memory.abstract: LSR-MP is a physics-informed message-passing framework that generalizes EGNNs by adding a fragmentation module (BRICS) and a long-range bipartite atom-fragment message-passing module to capture non-local interactions, achieving up to 40% MAE reduction on MD22/Chignolin while maintaining computational efficiency.

content.background: Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) driven by DFT is prohibitively expensive for large systems. Two existing approaches attempt to address this: (1) Fragmentation-based methods from quantum chemistry (e.g., MFCC, MIM, divide-and-conquer) decompose large molecules into subsystems for parallelized computation, but they fail to accurately capture many-body interactions beyond two- or three-body terms, limiting their accuracy to 1-5 kcal/mol. (2) Equivariant graph neural networks (EGNNs) such as PaiNN, ViSNet, Equiformer model many-body interactions within a local radius cutoff, achieving sub-1 kcal/mol accuracy on small molecules (MD17, QM9), but they suffer substantial information loss for larger molecules where long-range interactions (electrostatic, van der Waals) are non-negligible. Increasing the cutoff radius or stacking more layers to remedy this leads to information over-squashing, loss of data efficiency, and convergence difficulty. This creates a fundamental gap: fragmentation methods capture long-range but miss many-body; EGNNs capture many-body but miss long-range. LSR-MP bridges this gap by combining both approaches — using fragmentation to define coarse-grained interaction nodes and bipartite message-passing to efficiently propagate long-range information, while retaining the short-range EGNN for local many-body interactions.
content.method:
The LSR-MP framework operates at two levels on the input molecule:

**Short-Range Module**: Standard EGNN message-passing on a radius graph G_short (cutoff r_short ≈ 4-5Å), modeling local geometric information (bonds, angles, dihedrals). This produces scalar embeddings h and vectorial embeddings v for each atom. Any existing EGNN (ViSNet, PaiNN, Equiformer, ET) can serve as the short-range backbone.

**Fragmentation Module**: The molecule is fragmented using BRICS (Breaking of Retrosynthetically Interesting Chemical Substructures), which uses 16 predefined chemical motifs to break bonds at chemically meaningful positions, minimizing energy artifacts from bond breakage. Post-fragmentation processing removes small fragments, handles duplicates, and corrects overlaps. Fragment representations are learned from atom embeddings within each fragment: scalar H_j = Σ α_i ⊙ h_i, vectorial V_j = Σ β_i ⊙ v_i, position P_j = Σ γ_i p_i + κ_i ⊙ v_i, with SO(3)-invariant weights α,β,κ and translation-equivariant weights γ (Σγ_i=1, γ_i≥0). This ensures fragment embeddings are equivariant under SO(3) and translation.

**Long-Range Module**: Bipartite geometric message-passing on G_long (cutoff r_long ≈ 9Å, much larger than r_short) between atoms (set V) and fragments (set U). The key architectural component is a Distance-Dependent Bipartite Geometric Transformer: (1) Size-dependent distance encoding: r_ij = w(z_i, H_j)·dist(p_i, P_j) + b(z_i, H_j), then RBF expansion. (2) Multi-headed attention: query from atom scalar embeddings, key/value from fragment scalar embeddings, attention weights A_ij = SiLU(sum(q_i ⊙ k_j ⊙ s_ij)). (3) Scalar message: m_ij = DENSE(A_ij·v_j). (4) Vectorial message: m_ij = DENSE(A_ij·v_j) ⊙ (p_i-P_j)/||p_i-P_j|| + DENSE(A_ij·v_j) ⊙ V_j, combining directional and fragment-vectorial components. (5) Residual updates with scalar-vectorial interaction: x_i^l = x_i^{l-1} + LINEAR(m_i) ⊙ Û_i + LINEAR(m_i); μ_i^l = μ_i^{l-1} + m_i + LINEAR(m_i) ⊙ μ_i^{l-1}, where Û_i is the scalar product of vectorial embeddings under two projections (Proposition 4.1: Hadamard product of scalar×vectorial = vectorial; inner product of two vectorial = scalar).

**Output Fusion**: Late fusion strategy concatenates short-range and long-range embeddings: h_out = DENSE([h^L_short, x^L_long]), v_out = U([v^L_short, μ^L_long]). This preserves the complementary nature of local and non-local information.

**Theoretical Justification**: (1) From the many-body expansion perspective, short-range module captures ε_2, ε_3 within r_short; long-range module approximates higher-order interactions via atom-fragment bipartite interactions, where fragment descriptors summarize groups of distant atoms. (2) LSR-MP alleviates over-squashing: proved that the symmetric Jacobian obstruction O^(m)(v,u) is upper-bounded by 2ρ/(μc_α) independent of distance, versus the short-range bound of λτ(v,u) ≤ 2λ|E|^2 which grows quadratically with graph size. The bipartite graph rewiring reduces commute time by creating short paths through fragment virtual nodes. (3) BRICS prioritizes edges with high negative Balanced Forman curvature (bottleneck edges), confirmed by Mann-Whitney U-Test (p<0.001), which are exactly the edges causing over-squashing.
content.experiment:
**Datasets**: (1) MD22 — molecular dynamics trajectories of 5 biomolecules (Ac-Ala3-NHMe 42 atoms, DHA 56 atoms, Stachyose 87 atoms, AT-AT 60 atoms, AT-AT-CG-CG 118 atoms) plus 2 supramolecules (Buckyball catcher 148 atoms, Double-walled nanotube 370 atoms). Data split consistent with Chmiela et al. (2022). (2) Chignolin — 166-atom artificial protein, 9543 conformations from REMD at DFT level, split 7:1:2. (3) PubChemQC — molecules with MW>500 (40-100 atoms), 26000 train / 8000 test. (4) Electrostatics Binding Energy — 661 charged dimers with 13 configurations at varying distances (3-8Å), 600 train / 61 test.

**Baselines**: sGDML, PaiNN, TorchMD-NET, GemNet-OC, SO3krates, Allegro, MACE, Equiformer, ViSNet.

**Main Results (MD22 + Chignolin)**: ViSNet-LSRM achieves best or competitive energy/force MAE across all 5 biomolecules. On Chignolin (166 atoms), ViSNet-LSRM achieves energy MAE 1.2267 vs ViSNet 2.35, Equiformer 1.0967. On AT-AT-CG-CG (118 atoms), energy MAE 0.1064 vs ViSNet 0.1585, Equiformer 0.1510. Improvements scale with molecule size, confirming long-range importance.

**Efficiency**: At comparable force MAE (~0.13 on AT-AT-CG-CG), ViSNet-LSRM uses 1.70M parameters vs Allegro 15.11M, Equiformer 3.02M, ViSNet 2.21M; training time 19s/epoch vs Allegro 818s, Equiformer 155s, ViSNet 44s.

**Over-Squashing Study**: (Q1) Increasing short-range cutoff beyond 4-5Å deteriorates performance for all EGNNs (ViSNet, PaiNN, ViSNet-LSRM short-range component), confirming information over-squashing from too many neighbors. (Q2) Increasing layer depth improves performance but a 3-layer ViSNet-LSRM outperforms 8-layer ViSNet, showing explicit long-range modules are more effective than deepening. Shallow ViSNet-LSRM is also more efficient.

**Ablation (AT-AT-CG-CG)**: BRICS fragmentation (avg size 8.43): energy 0.1064, force 0.1135. K-Means (avg size 8.43): energy 0.1276, force 0.1246. Single global node: energy 0.1482, force 0.1696. Without long-range: energy 0.1563, force 0.1995. BRICS > K-Means > Global Node > No long-range, confirming both the importance of long-range components and the superiority of chemistry-informed fragmentation.

**General Applicability**: LSR-MP applied to PaiNN, ET, Equiformer, ViSNet (4 short-range + 2 long-range vs 6-layer baseline). Force MAE reductions: Equiformer -15%, ViSNet -24.88%, PaiNN -58.8%, ET -55% on AT-AT-CG-CG.

**Additional Experiments**: Electrostatics binding energy MAE: ViSNet-LSRM 0.0654 vs ViSNet 0.1064 (38% reduction). PubChem: ViSNet-LSRM 2.012 vs ViSNet 2.978. Transferability: few-shot (50 samples) ViSNet-LSRM energy 2.167 vs ViSNet 2.575. MD simulation: 200ps NVE shows energy conservation within 0.0001%. Long-range cutoff ablation: optimal at 9Å, larger cutoffs don't hurt (few fragments prevent over-squashing).
content.result:
LSR-MP achieves significant and consistent improvements across multiple EGNN backbones and datasets, with improvements scaling with molecule size — confirming that long-range interactions become increasingly important for larger systems. The framework is a true generalization of EGNNs (reducible to standard EGNN when r_long = r_short) and adds long-range capability without sacrificing many-body accuracy or computational efficiency. Key findings: (1) Simply increasing cutoff or depth in standard EGNNs causes over-squashing and diminishing returns; explicit long-range modules via bipartite message-passing are far more effective. (2) BRICS fragmentation outperforms naive clustering because it breaks bonds at chemically meaningful positions (high negative curvature edges), creating fragments that preserve intrinsic chemical environments and simultaneously alleviate graph bottleneck structure. (3) The bipartite atom-fragment interaction model is computationally efficient because the number of fragments is small relative to atoms, preventing the neighbor explosion that causes over-squashing in extended cutoff approaches.

**Limitations**: BRICS fails on supramolecules (Buckyball catcher, Double-walled nanotube) that don't match its 16 predefined chemical motifs; K-Means/spectral clustering must be used as alternatives with reduced performance. The fragmentation is non-differentiable, preventing end-to-end optimization of fragment boundaries. Future work should develop differentiable fragmentation methods.

**Relevance to broader field**: LSR-MP provides a principled solution to the over-squashing problem in molecular GNNs by rewiring the graph through chemistry-informed virtual nodes (fragments). This is analogous to virtual node approaches in general GNN literature but with domain-specific grounding. The theoretical analysis connecting BRICS to negative curvature edges and the Jacobian obstruction bound provides rigorous justification.
content.dataset: MD22, Chignolin, PubChemQC, Electrostatics Binding Energy
content.topic_relation: Touches H4 (Representation-Usage Gap) and H5 (Architecture-Dependent Periodicity Encoding). LSR-MP demonstrates that the over-squashing problem in local MPNNs can be solved not by deepening or widening, but by rewiring the graph with domain-informed virtual nodes (fragments). This is directly relevant to polymer periodicity: polymer repeat units create long-range dependencies across the chain that local GIN message-passing cannot propagate. The BRICS fragmentation concept parallels the idea of treating polymer repeat units as 'fragments' for long-range interaction modeling. The bipartite atom-fragment message-passing could be adapted to polymer periodic graphs where repeat-unit-level virtual nodes enable non-local information flow.
content.topic_contribution: Provides an actionable architecture pattern for polymer long-range interaction: (1) Use repeat-unit boundaries as fragmentation points (analogous to BRICS but periodicity-informed), creating fragment virtual nodes. (2) Implement bipartite message-passing between atom nodes and repeat-unit fragment nodes to capture non-local periodicity effects. (3) This could address the 50→30 representation-usage gap by giving GIN a mechanism to USE periodicity knowledge through fragment-level attention, rather than relying on pre-training alone. (4) The over-squashing theoretical analysis (Jacobian obstruction bound) provides a formal justification for why periodic virtual nodes help — they reduce commute time between distant atoms in the polymer chain. (5) The finding that increasing cutoff/depth fails but bipartite rewiring succeeds suggests that polymer architectures should focus on graph topology modification (adding periodic virtual nodes) rather than model depth or neighbor expansion.

memory.abstract: SPSE replaces RWSE in graph transformers by encoding edges via simple path counts rather than random walk probabilities, theoretically overcoming RWSE's inability to distinguish cycles from paths and enabling cycle counting for adjacent nodes, with an approximate DFS+BFS DAG decomposition algorithm for tractable computation.

content.background: Graph transformers leverage global self-attention to overcome the localized message-passing limitations of GNNs, but require suitable positional and structural encodings to capture graph irregularities. Random Walk Structural Encoding (RWSE) has emerged as a popular edge encoding method, encoding both structural and positional information via random walk landing probabilities between node pairs. RWSE is computationally efficient (closed-form via matrix powers) and has shown substantial improvements in state-of-the-art graph transformers (GRIT, CSA). However, RWSE has fundamental expressivity limitations: it cannot distinguish edges belonging to different local graph patterns in certain cases. Specifically, Proposition 1 proves that any pair of nodes in an even-length cycle graph has identical RWSE encoding to some pair in a path graph — random walk probabilities cannot differentiate cyclic from linear topology at the edge level. Proposition 2 further shows that RWSE encoding of any node pair is never unique; for any graph and node pair, there exists a non-isomorphic graph with an equivalent RWSE encoding. These ambiguities arise because random walks measure probabilities (normalized by degree) rather than absolute counts, diluting structural information. This motivates exploring simple paths (self-avoiding walks) as a richer structural encoding, since parallel work on MPNNs has demonstrated that path-based methods exceed 1-WL expressivity (Michel et al., 2023; Graziani et al., 2024). The challenge is computational: exact simple path counting is intractable for large graphs and long path lengths, requiring efficient approximation methods.
content.method: SPSE encodes graph structure by counting simple paths of varying lengths between node pairs, replacing the random walk probability matrix P with the simple path count matrix S in graph transformer edge encoding. The core theoretical advantage is Proposition 3: for adjacent nodes (i,j) with (S_k)_ij = m_k, there are exactly m_k cycles of length k+1 containing edge (i,j). This means SPSE directly characterizes the cyclic structures to which each edge belongs — a property RWSE fundamentally lacks since landing probabilities can be made arbitrarily low by adding edges to cycle nodes. This is crucial for applications like molecular chemistry (aromatic rings), social networks (communities), and circuit design (feedback loops). The encoding procedure follows three steps: (1) Path Counting: Compute S = [S_1,...,S_K] where S_k gives the number of simple paths of length k between all node pairs. Since exact counting is #P-hard and impractical for large graphs, an approximate algorithm based on successive DAG decompositions is proposed. Starting from selected root nodes (proportion R of |V|), the algorithm decomposes the undirected graph into directed acyclic graphs via a combined DFS+BFS strategy: DFS explores deep paths from the root up to depth D_DFS, then partial BFS randomly explores a subset of child nodes (enabling discovery of multiple paths between same nodes), followed by full BFS to cover remaining nodes. Each DAG yields a node ordering; directing edges toward higher-index nodes creates a nilpotent adjacency matrix whose powers give path counts for that DAG. Multiple DAG decompositions (controlled by trial number N and root proportion R) explore different paths, and counts are updated by taking the maximum across all DAGs — yielding lower bounds on exact counts. Complexity is O(K*R*D_DFS*N*|V|^3), dominated by matrix power computations per DAG. (2) Path Count Encoding: Raw counts can grow exponentially, so a composition of logarithmic functions maps them to a manageable range: f(x) = α·g^n(x) + β where g(x) = ln(1+x), with α, β, n as dataset-specific hyperparameters. Denser graphs require higher n or lower α for compression. (3) Edge Encoding Integration: The normalized path count matrix f(S) replaces the random walk matrix P as input to the shallow neural network φ_0 that produces the edge encoding matrix E_SP, which substitutes E_RW in the self-attention equations (a_ij = φ_1(W^Q x_i, W^K x_j, E_ij) and y_i = Σ_j α_ij φ_2(W^V x_j, E_ij)). SPSE is a drop-in replacement for RWSE with no change in trainable parameters.
content.experiment: Experiments span three benchmark categories: (1) Synthetic cycle counting: 12,000 graphs with randomly added cycles of lengths 3-8, task is six simultaneous multiclass classification tasks counting cycles per length. CSA and GRIT with SPSE vs RWSE across three model configurations (40-280 gigaflops). SPSE achieves significantly higher accuracy in all but one case, validating Proposition 3 empirically. (2) Real-world benchmarks: ZINC (MAE), Peptides-functional (AP), Peptides-structural (MAE), PCQM4Mv2 (MAE) for molecular graphs; PATTERN and CLUSTER (accuracy) for SBM; MNIST and CIFAR10 (accuracy) for superpixels. Three model architectures tested: GPS (SPSE used only in MPNN for node PE, restricted to edges in ε), CSA (SPSE as full edge encoding in self-attention), GRIT (SPSE as full edge encoding). All models retrained on 10 random seeds (1 for PCQM4Mv2) using released configurations with no hyperparameter tuning — isolating SPSE's contribution as a fair drop-in replacement. Two-sided Student's t-tests assess significance. Path counting hyperparameters vary per dataset: molecular datasets use R=100%, moderate K (15-23), low N (1); SBM uses R=40%, N=7; superpixels use R=55%, N=2. Preprocessing times range from 1hr (ZINC) to 80hr (CIFAR10, PCQM4Mv2). (3) Ablation on path count sensitivity: Varying R, D_DFS, N individually on ZINC, PATTERN, MNIST. For ZINC, R is the dominant parameter (can be set to 100% cheaply); D_DFS and N have little impact. For MNIST, all three contribute roughly equally. For PATTERN (dense SBM), N is most cost-effective for improving path discovery. Key finding: MNIST with N=2 discovers ~40% fewer paths than N=8, potentially limiting accuracy.
content.result: SPSE improves performance in 21 out of 24 cases compared to RWSE. The most notable gains are on molecular graphs with pure graph transformers (CSA and GRIT): statistically significant improvements in 5 of 6 molecular cases (ZINC MAE 0.061 vs 0.069 for CSA, 0.059 vs 0.065 for GRIT; Peptides-func AP 0.6605 vs 0.6513 for CSA, 0.6945 vs 0.6803 for GRIT; Peptides-struct MAE 0.2449 vs 0.2480 for GRIT). Superpixel benchmarks show 2 significant improvements. GPS with SPSE shows limited improvement because it restricts encoding to edges in ε (reducing dimensionality of existing embeddings when parameters are kept unchanged) rather than using the full structural matrix in self-attention. CLUSTER (dense SBM) shows no significant improvement for pure transformers, likely because approximate path counts underestimate in highly connected graphs. The fundamental limitation is that the max-update strategy yields lower bounds on exact counts, and in dense graphs, many paths cannot be discovered simultaneously by any single DAG decomposition (illustrated by a failure case where two length-4 paths require a non-acyclic directed graph). This suggests trading longer path lengths for exact shorter-path counts may be preferable in dense graphs. Future directions include optimizing computational efficiency, hierarchical methods for efficient long-range path mining, and extending to knowledge graphs and large social networks.
content.dataset: ZINC, Peptides-functional, Peptides-structural, PCQM4Mv2, PATTERN, CLUSTER, MNIST, CIFAR10, synthetic cycle counting dataset
content.topic_relation: Directly relates to H2 (Architecture-SSL Co-Design) and H5 (Architecture-Dependent Periodicity Encoding). SPSE was tested on Day 2 as GPS-SPSE-Trimer (54.41 RMSE, FAILED) confirming the Small-Graph Paradox — Transformer attention is redundant on small polymer graphs where MPNN already reaches all nodes. The paper's theoretical cycle-counting insight (Proposition 3) is relevant to polymer periodicity: simple path counts between adjacent nodes directly enumerate cycles containing that edge, which could characterize aromatic rings and periodic unit boundaries in polymer graphs. The paper also validates that structural encoding effectiveness depends on how it is used in the architecture (GPS restricted to ε vs CSA/GRIT full self-attention), consistent with H5.
content.topic_contribution: Provides three actionable insights: (1) Theoretical validation that simple path counts capture cycle structure that random walks cannot — this supports using path-based features (LiGhT-style) as explicit periodicity encodings for polymer GNNs, bypassing the Transformer overhead that caused GPS-SPSE failure. (2) Confirms that structural encoding must match architecture: SPSE works best when used as full pairwise encoding in self-attention (CSA/GRIT), not restricted to edge set ε (GPS). For polymer GIN, path counts should be explicit node/edge features, not attention biases. (3) The approximate path counting algorithm (DFS+BFS DAG decomposition) could be adapted to compute periodic-path features for polymer unit cells as a preprocessing step, providing cycle-aware structural features without requiring Transformer architecture. However, the Small-Graph Paradox and dense-graph limitations warn against applying SPSE directly to polymer trimers via Transformer — the path features should instead feed into simple MPNN architectures.

memory.abstract: LSR-MP is a physics-informed message-passing framework that combines fragmentation-based methods (BRICS) with equivariant GNNs via bipartite atom-fragment long-range message passing, addressing both long-range interaction capture and many-body interaction modeling for scalable molecular dynamics, achieving up to 40% MAE reduction on MD22/Chignolin.

content.background: Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) driven by DFT is prohibitively expensive for large systems. Two approaches have been developed to address this: (1) fragmentation-based methods from quantum chemistry, which subdivide large molecules into smaller subsystems for parallelized computation, and (2) machine learning force fields, particularly equivariant graph neural networks (EGNNs) that incorporate symmetry inductive bias. However, each approach has critical limitations. Fragmentation-based methods rely on the principle of chemical locality — that subsystems exhibit minimal interactions — but the many-body interactions among subsystems (two-body, three-body corrections) are the primary source of error, and truncating the many-body expansion compromises accuracy to 1-5 kcal/mol. EGNNs model interactions within a predefined radius cutoff, effectively capturing local many-body interactions (bonds, angles, dihedrals) but losing long-range interactions (electrostatic, van der Waals) that become non-negligible for larger molecules. Naively increasing the cutoff radius or stacking more layers to capture long-range information leads to information over-squashing, loss of data efficiency, and convergence difficulty. This creates a fundamental tension: fragmentation methods capture long-range but miss many-body; EGNNs capture many-body but miss long-range. LSR-MP bridges this gap by introducing fragmentation-based message passing on top of EGNNs, creating a dual-level architecture that explicitly models both short-range many-body and long-range interactions efficiently.
content.method:
The LSR-MP framework consists of three modules operating at two levels:

**Short-Range Module**: Operates on a radius graph G_short with cutoff r_short (typically 4-5Å), performing standard equivariant message passing to model local geometric information (bonds, angles, dihedrals). This module uses any EGNN backbone (ViSNet, PaiNN, Equiformer, etc.) and produces scalar embeddings h and vectorial embeddings v for each atom. The iterative update follows: h_i^l, v_i^l = φ_Short(h_i^{l-1}, v_i^{l-1}, Σ m_ij, Σ m_ij_vec).

**Fragmentation Module**: Uses BRICS (Breaking of Retrosynthetically Interesting Chemical Substructures) from RDKit to fragment the molecule into chemically meaningful substructures. BRICS employs 16 predefined chemical motifs selected by organic chemists, breaking bonds at chemically appropriate locations to minimize energy discrepancies from bond breakages. Post-fragmentation processing removes small fragments, handles duplicates, and corrects overlaps. Fragment representations are learned by summarizing atom embeddings within each fragment: H_j = Σ α_i ⊙ h_i (scalar), V_j = Σ β_i ⊙ v_i (vectorial), P_j = Σ γ_i p_i + κ_i ⊙ v_i (position). The weights α, β, κ are SO(3)-invariant, and γ_i satisfies Σ γ_i = 1, γ_i ≥ 0 for translational equivariance. Fragment vectorial embeddings enable equivariant long-range interaction modeling.

**Long-Range Module**: Performs bipartite geometric message passing between atoms and fragments on a radius graph G_long with cutoff r_long (much larger than r_short, typically 9Å). The edge set connects atoms to fragments within distance r_long. The key design is a distance-dependent equivariant multi-headed attention mechanism: (1) Size-dependent distance encoding: r_ij = w(z_i, H_j)·dist(p_i, P_j) + b(z_i, H_j), processed through RBF + dense layer. (2) Attention: A_ij = SiLU(sum(q_i ⊙ k_j ⊙ s_ij)), where query from atom scalar embeddings, key/value from fragment scalar embeddings. (3) Scalar message: m_ij = Dense(A_ij · v_j). (4) Vectorial message: m_ij_vec = Dense(A_ij · v_j) ⊙ (p_i - P_j)/||p_i - P_j|| + Dense(A_ij · v_j) ⊙ V_j, combining directional and fragment vectorial information. (5) Update: x_i^l = x_i^{l-1} + Linear(m_i) ⊙ U(v_i) + Linear(m_i); μ_i^l = μ_i^{l-1} + m_i_vec + Linear(m_i) ⊙ μ_i^{l-1}. Layer normalization and norm-based min-max normalization are applied to fragment embeddings for convergence stability.

**Late Fusion Strategy**: Short-range (h, v) and long-range (x, μ) embeddings are concatenated and fused: h_out = Dense([h^{L_short}, x^{L_long}]), v_out = U([v^{L_short}, μ^{L_long}]). This preserves the complementary information from both levels.

**Theoretical Foundation**: (1) The framework is a generalization of EGNNs — setting r_long = r_short reduces it to standard EGNN. (2) The energy decomposition ansatz E_tot = Σ e^(1) + Σ e^(2) + Σ e^(3) + ... is approximated with two truncation radii: short-range interactions use ε functions, long-range interactions use ε' functions approximated via atom-fragment interactions rather than atom-atom (for computational efficiency). (3) BRICS prioritizes edges with high negative Balanced Forman curvature — these are bottleneck edges causing over-squashing. The long-range module rewires the graph to alleviate these bottlenecks. (4) Proved that LSR-MP improves the upper bound of the Jacobian obstruction (symmetric Jacobian obstruction from Di Giovanni et al.): the long-range module bounds O^(m)(v,u) ≤ 2ρ/(μc_α), independent of distance, versus the short-range module's O(|E|²) bound dependent on commute time.
content.experiment:
**Datasets**: (1) MD22 — 5 large biomolecules (Ac-Ala3-NHMe 42 atoms, DHA 56 atoms, Stachyose 87 atoms, AT-AT 60 atoms, AT-AT-CG-CG 118 atoms) plus 2 supramolecules (Buckyball catcher 148 atoms, Double-walled nanotube 370 atoms). Data split consistent with Chmiela et al. (2022). (2) Chignolin — 166-atom artificial protein, 9543 conformations from REMD at DFT level, split 7:1:2. (3) Electrostatics Binding Energy — 661 charged molecular dimers with 13 configurations each (3-8Å distances), 600 train/61 test. (4) PubChemQC — molecules with MW>500 (40-100 atoms), 26000 train/8000 test.

**Baselines**: sGDML, PaiNN, TorchMD-NET, GemNetOC, SO3krates, Allegro, MACE, Equiformer, ViSNet.

**Main Results (MD22 + Chignolin)**: ViSNet-LSRM achieves state-of-the-art on most molecules. On AT-AT-CG-CG: energy MAE 0.1335 (vs ViSNet 0.1585, Equiformer 0.1510), force MAE 0.1064 (vs ViSNet 0.1283). On Chignolin: energy MAE 1.2267 (vs ViSNet 2.35, Equiformer 1.0967). Up to 40% MAE reduction. Improvements more pronounced for larger molecules, confirming long-range interaction importance.

**Efficiency Comparison**: At comparable force MAE (~0.13 on AT-AT-CG-CG), ViSNet-LSRM uses 1.70M parameters and 19s/epoch vs Allegro 15.11M/818s and Equiformer 3.02M/155s. 2.3x faster than ViSNet baseline.

**Long-Range Interaction Studies**: (1) Increasing short-range cutoff beyond 4-5Å significantly deteriorates performance for all EGNNs (over-squashing). (2) Increasing layers improves performance but a 3-layer ViSNet-LSRM outperforms 8-layer ViSNet — explicit long-range modules are more effective than deepening. (3) Ablation: BRICS (energy 0.1064, force 0.1135) > K-Means (0.1276, 0.1246) > Single Global Node (0.1482, 0.1696) > No long-range (0.1563, 0.1995). Even K-means LSR-MP surpasses baseline without long-range, confirming long-range component importance. BRICS outperforms K-means due to chemical insight.

**General Applicability**: LSR-MP applied to PaiNN, ET, Equiformer, ViSNet (4 short-range + 2 long-range vs 6-layer baseline). Force MAE reductions: Equiformer 15%, ViSNet 24.88%, PaiNN 58.8%, ET 55.0% on AT-AT-CG-CG.

**Electrostatics Binding Energy**: ViSNet-LSRM 0.0654 vs ViSNet 0.1064 (38% reduction), demonstrating better long-range electrostatic capture. Decay curves show more physically appropriate decaying behavior.

**Transferability**: Zero-shot from smaller MD22 molecules to AT-AT-CG-CG: ViSNet-LSRM 150.23 vs ViSNet 184.44. Few-shot (50 samples): ViSNet-LSRM 2.167 vs ViSNet 2.575. PubChem (train <60 atoms, test >60): ViSNet-LSRM 3.339 vs ViSNet 4.458.

**MD Simulation**: 20ps NVE simulation of AT-AT shows similar vibrational spectra to DFT. 200ps simulation shows energy conservation within ±0.0001%.

**Geometric Optimization**: ViSNet-LSRM achieves up to 50% reduction in DFT iterations for hybrid GO, with lower RMSD to reference geometry.
content.result: LSR-MP achieves significant and consistent improvements across multiple EGNN backbones and datasets, with the most pronounced gains on larger molecules where long-range interactions are critical. The framework's success stems from three synergistic mechanisms: (1) BRICS fragmentation provides chemically meaningful coarse-graining that preserves intrinsic chemical structures, reducing artifacts from bond breaking and creating informative fragment representations; (2) Bipartite atom-fragment message passing efficiently captures long-range interactions without the computational cost of all-atom long-range modeling (O(N^1-2) vs O(N^3+)); (3) The long-range module rewires negatively curved bottleneck edges identified by BRICS, alleviating over-squashing both empirically and theoretically (proved upper bound improvement on Jacobian obstruction). Key findings: increasing cutoff or depth in standard EGNNs does NOT solve long-range interaction capture (over-squashing and convergence issues); explicit long-range modules are more effective and efficient than deepening; BRICS outperforms naive clustering because chemical locality priors guide fragmentation toward informative substructures. Limitations: BRICS fails on supramolecules (non-organic chemical prototypes), requiring fallback to K-means/spectral clustering; the fragmentation is non-differentiable (fixed preprocessing). Future work: differentiable fragmentation learned end-to-end. For the polymer domain, this paper's insight that explicit long-range/periodic modules outperform naive depth/cutoff increases directly validates H4 (representation-usage gap) — local MPNNs cannot USE long-range information regardless of depth, requiring architectural modifications like bipartite message passing or periodic edge handling.

memory.abstract: LSR-MP is a physics-informed framework generalizing EGNNs to capture long-range interactions via BRICS fragmentation and bipartite atom-fragment message passing, achieving up to 40% MAE reduction on large biomolecules while maintaining computational efficiency and showing general applicability across multiple EGNN backbones.

content.background: Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) driven by DFT is prohibitively expensive for large systems. Two existing approaches attempt to address this: (1) Fragmentation-based methods from quantum chemistry subdivide molecules into subsystems for parallel computation, but their accuracy is limited by truncation of many-body interactions (typically only two- or three-body terms are included, introducing errors of 1-5 kcal/mol). (2) Equivariant graph neural networks (EGNNs) model many-body interactions within a local cutoff radius but fundamentally miss long-range interactions (electrostatic, van der Waals forces) that become non-negligible for larger molecules. Naive remedies — increasing the cutoff radius or stacking more layers — cause information over-squashing, loss of data efficiency, and convergence difficulty. This creates a fundamental gap: fragmentation methods capture long-range but miss many-body; EGNNs capture many-body but miss long-range. LSR-MP bridges this gap by combining both approaches, using fragmentation to define coarse-grained long-range interaction channels while preserving fine-grained many-body modeling through the short-range EGNN module.
content.method:
LSR-MP operates at two levels with three modules:

1. **Short-Range Module**: Standard EGNN message passing on a radius graph G_short with cutoff r_short (typically 4-5Å). Processes atomic numbers Z and positions p to produce scalar embeddings h and vectorial embeddings v, modeling local geometric information (bonds, angles, dihedrals). This is the many-body interaction encoder.

2. **Fragmentation Module**: Uses BRICS (Breaking of Retrosynthetically Interesting Chemical Substructures) from RDKit to fragment molecules into chemically meaningful substructures based on 16 predefined chemical motifs. This preserves intrinsic chemical structures and minimizes artifacts from bond breaking. Fragment representations are learned from atom embeddings: scalar H_j = Σ α_i ⊙ h_i, vectorial V_j = Σ β_i ⊙ v_i, and position P_j = Σ γ_i p_i + κ_i ⊙ v_i (with Σ γ_i = 1 for translational equivariance). The vectorial fragment embeddings enable equivariant long-range interaction modeling.

3. **Long-Range Module**: Performs bipartite geometric message passing on G_long between atoms and fragments with cutoff r_long (much larger than r_short, typically 9Å). Uses a distance-dependent equivariant multi-headed attention mechanism: query from atom scalar embeddings, key/value from fragment scalar embeddings, attention weights modulated by size-dependent distance encoding (radial basis functions with linear correction for fragment/atom size). Vectorial messages combine relative direction (p_i - P_j)/||p_i - P_j|| and fragment vectorial embeddings V_j, gated by attention. Scalar and vectorial embeddings are updated with residual connections incorporating inner products of vectorial embeddings under different projections (maintaining equivariance via Proposition 4.1: Hadamard product of scalar×vectorial = vectorial; inner product of two vectorial = scalar).

4. **Late Fusion**: Short-range (h, v) and long-range (x, μ) embeddings are concatenated and projected: h_out = DENSE([h^L_short, x^L_long]), v_out = U([v^L_short, μ^L_long]).

**Theoretical Foundation**: LSR-MP alleviates over-squashing by reducing commute time in the computational graph. In standard EGNNs, the symmetric Jacobian obstruction O^(m)(v,u) is bounded by λτ(v,u) where τ is commute time that can be O(|E|²) for elongated molecules. With LSR-MP's bipartite graph (each atom connected to fragment virtual nodes), commute time is bounded by 4|E|, giving O^(m)(v,u) ≤ 2ρ/(μc_α) — independent of spatial distance. BRICS fragmentation prioritizes edges with high negative Balanced Forman curvature (bottleneck edges between functional groups), effectively rewiring the graph to alleviate over-squashing at these critical points.
content.experiment:
**Datasets**: MD22 (5 large biomolecules: Ac-Ala3-NHMe 42 atoms, DHA 56 atoms, Stachyose 87 atoms, AT-AT 60 atoms, AT-AT-CG-CG 118 atoms), Chignolin (166 atoms, 9543 conformations from REMD at DFT level), PubChemQC (85.9M small molecules, subset with MW>500), Electrostatics Binding Energy (661 charged dimers).

**ViSNet-LSRM Results on MD22 + Chignolin**: ViSNet-LSRM achieves competitive or superior performance vs. Equiformer, Allegro, MACE, SO3krates, GemNetOC. On AT-AT-CG-CG: energy MAE 0.1335 (vs ViSNet 0.1585, Equiformer ~0.15), force MAE 0.0632 (vs ViSNet 0.0869). On Chignolin: energy MAE 1.2267 (vs ViSNet 2.35, Equiformer 1.0967). Up to 40% MAE reduction over baseline ViSNet, with improvement more pronounced for larger molecules.

**Efficiency**: ViSNet-LSRM uses 1.70M parameters (vs ViSNet 2.21M, Equiformer 3.02M, Allegro 15.11M) and 19s/epoch (vs ViSNet 44s, Equiformer 155s, Allegro 818s) at comparable force MAE on AT-AT-CG-CG.

**Long-Range Interaction Studies**: (1) Increasing short-range cutoff beyond 4-5Å deteriorates performance across all EGNNs (over-squashing). (2) Increasing depth helps but 3-layer ViSNet-LSRM outperforms 8-layer ViSNet — explicit long-range modules more effective than deepening. (3) Ablation: BRICS > K-Means > Single Global Node > No long-range component. BRICS fragmentation outperforms K-Means because it preserves chemical structure and prioritizes negative-curvature bottleneck edges.

**General Applicability**: LSR-MP applied to PaiNN, ET, Equiformer, ViSNet backbones (4 short-range + 2 long-range layers vs 6-layer baseline). Force MAE reductions: Equiformer 15%, ViSNet 24.88%, PaiNN 58.8%, ET 55.0% on AT-AT-CG-CG.

**Additional Experiments**: Electrostatics binding energy MAE 0.0654 (vs ViSNet 0.1064). PubChem large molecules energy MAE 2.012 (vs 2.978). Transferability: few-shot learning and PubChem cross-size experiments show improvement. MD simulation of AT-AT for 20ps shows similar vibrational spectra to DFT; 200ps NVE simulation shows energy conservation within 0.0001%.
content.result:
LSR-MP successfully bridges the long-range/many-body gap by combining fragmentation-based coarse-graining with EGNN fine-grained modeling. The bipartite atom-fragment architecture is the key design choice: it avoids the over-squashing problem of increasing cutoff/depth in standard EGNNs while maintaining O(N^a) computational efficiency (a=1~2). The BRICS fragmentation provides two-fold benefits: (1) chemical insight for meaningful fragment representations, and (2) graph rewiring at negative-curvature bottleneck edges. The theoretical proof that LSR-MP bounds the Jacobian obstruction independent of spatial distance formalizes the over-squashing alleviation.

**Limitations**: BRICS fails on supramolecules (Buckyball catcher, Double-walled nanotube) that don't match its 16 chemical motifs, requiring fallback to K-Means or spectral clustering. The fragmentation is non-differentiable and not learned end-to-end. Fragment size has an optimal range — too small fragments increase computational cost, too large fragments lose long-range resolution.

**Future Directions**: Differentiable fragmentation for end-to-end learning of optimal partitions. Extension to periodic/condensed-phase systems. The framework's general applicability across EGNN backbones suggests it could become a standard augmentation for molecular property prediction on large systems.

**Relevance to polymer deep learning**: Polymer repeat units are inherently fragmented structures (monomers connected by bonds). The bipartite atom-fragment message passing paradigm could be adapted for periodic polymer graphs, where fragments correspond to repeat units and long-range interactions capture inter-unit periodicity effects. The over-squashing analysis is particularly relevant for polymer chains where commute time between distant units is O(|E|²).

content.topic_contribution: Provides three actionable insights: (1) Over-squashing formalization — commute time analysis proves why local MPNNs fail on elongated/periodic structures, supporting the pivot from 'learn periodicity' to 'use periodicity' via architectural rewiring. (2) Bipartite atom-fragment paradigm — could be adapted for polymer graphs where repeat units are fragments and inter-unit interactions are long-range edges, potentially addressing the 50→30 gap by enabling cross-unit information flow without over-squashing. (3) BRICS-like chemical fragmentation for polymers — repeat unit boundaries are natural fragmentation points; this suggests a polymer-specific LSR-MP where fragments = monomers and long-range module captures periodic coupling. This could be combined with Bloch spectral features as fragment-level representations.

content.root_cause_analysis: The fundamental bottleneck is near-degenerate h_pre representations. The monomer-level GIN encoder (even with PA contrastive pre-training) produces nearly identical 256-dim vectors for ALL 7170 polymers (mean cos_sim=0.963). This means: (1) The 'prompt' carries almost no discriminative information — it cannot condition the prediction because all polymers get the same prompt. (2) Monomer graphs are too small (~10-20 nodes) and too structurally similar for contrastive pre-training to produce diverse representations. (3) The periodicity information is in the INTER-RU structure (trimer-level), not within a single monomer. A monomer-level encoder cannot capture periodicity by definition — it sees only one RU.

hypothesis_conclusion.H4a: NOT SUPPORTED — prompt conditioning cannot bridge the representation-usage gap when the prompt itself is degenerate. The mechanism is sound in principle (frozen conditioning signal) but fails in practice because the monomer-level encoder produces non-discriminative representations.
hypothesis_conclusion.H4b: WEAKLY EVIDENCED — PCFT reduces overfitting gap (18.59 vs 29.95) suggesting the frozen prompt provides regularization, but test RMSE is not improved. Dual-channel structure hurts without meaningful prompt (random-init PCFT=53.34 > baseline=52.46).

content.overfitting_gap_insight: PCFT consistently reduces overfitting gap across all variants: baseline=29.95, PCFT=18.59, both-frozen=13.83. The frozen h_pre acts as a regularizer by preventing the fine-tuning encoder from memorizing training data as aggressively. However, this regularization comes at the cost of reduced model capacity — the train RMSE increases from 22.51 (baseline) to 34.13 (PCFT), meaning the model learns less from training data. The net effect is slightly worse test RMSE (52.72 vs 52.46).
meta_method_lessons: Degenerate Prompt Lesson: A frozen conditioning signal is useless if it carries no discriminative information. Mean pairwise cos_sim=0.963 means the prompt is essentially a constant vector — it cannot differentiate between polymers. Before implementing prompt mechanisms, verify that the prompt representations are diverse and discriminative.

Monomer Encoder Limitation: Monomer-level GIN encoders cannot produce discriminative representations for Tg prediction because (a) monomers are too small for diverse representations, and (b) periodicity is an INTER-RU phenomenon that cannot be captured by a single-RU encoder. This is a fundamental architectural limitation, not a training issue.

Regularization vs Capacity Trade-off: Reducing overfitting gap does NOT necessarily improve test RMSE. PCFT reduced overfitting gap by ~11 points but test RMSE increased by 0.26 points. The model needs BOTH regularization AND capacity — removing capacity (via frozen prompt) to reduce overfitting is counterproductive when the prompt carries no useful information.

Dual-Encoder Noise: Adding a second encoder with random initialization (no pre-training) introduces noise that hurts performance (53.34 vs 52.46). The dual-encoder structure is only beneficial if the frozen encoder carries meaningful, discriminative information.

comparison_with_previous.note: Day 1 used sum_pool (50.19), Day 4 uses mean_pool (52.46). The pooling method accounts for ~2 RMSE difference. PCFT with mean_pool (52.72) is comparable to PerioGT-Lite (52.92) — both are in the same performance range, confirming that pre-training provides regularization but not discriminative improvement.

content.next_direction: The PCFT mechanism is sound but the monomer-level prompt is degenerate. Options: (1) Use TRIMER-level encoder for both channels (h_pre from frozen trimer encoder, h_task from fine-tuning trimer encoder) — but this removes the monomer-trimer asymmetry that PCFT relies on. (2) BlochSpec (mem_120) — shift periodicity from representation space to input space via computed spectral features, bypassing the representation-usage gap entirely. (3) Chemprop-Polymer (mem_119) — architecture-periodicity matching with directed bond messages on periodic graphs. The monomer encoder limitation suggests that periodicity must be encoded either as input features (BlochSpec) or through architecture-periodicity matching (Chemprop), not through learned representations from small monomer graphs.

memory.content:
BlochSpec Experiment — Day 4, Experiment 2

**Idea**: Shift periodicity from learned representation space (where GIN can't use it) to computed input-space features. Compute Bloch band structure of chemistry-weighted periodic Laplacian as 12 deterministic spectral summary features, concatenate with GNN embedding in prediction head.

**Hypotheses Tested**:
- H1 (Input-space periodicity bypasses representation-usage gap): NOT SUPPORTED
- H2 (Bloch band structure encodes Tg-relevant physics): PARTIALLY SUPPORTED (features have genuine Tg correlations, but redundant with GNN)
- H3 (Chemistry-weighted Laplacian captures both topology and chemistry): NOT SUPPORTED

**Results (global_mean_pool, seeds={42,71,123}, mean±std)**:
| Experiment | Test RMSE | Delta vs Baseline | Significant? |
| Baseline GIN+Trimer | 51.71 ± 0.33 | baseline | --- |
| BlochSpec (GIN+Bloch) | 53.25 ± 0.51 | +1.54 (WORSE) | NO (p=0.113) |
| GIN+WiderMLP (param ctrl) | 51.37 ± 1.76 | -0.34 | NO (p=0.789) |
| ReducedGNN+Bloch (dim ctrl) | 53.49 ± 0.10 | +1.78 (WORSE) | YES (p=0.028) |
| Pure Spectral MLP | 76.71 ± 1.26 | +25.00 (much worse) | YES |
| GIN + Random Features | 52.11 ± 0.57 | +0.40 (WORSE) | NO (p=0.349) |
| GIN + Unweighted Lap | 51.89 ± 2.18 | +0.18 | NO (p=0.927) |

**Spectral Feature-Tg Correlations** (pre-training diagnostic):
- low_freq_density: r=-0.64 (strongest)
- spectral_centroid: r=+0.58
- spectral_gap: r=-0.47
- 9/12 features have |r| > 0.2

**Critical Findings**:
1. Bloch features have genuine Tg-relevant signal (correlations up to r=-0.64), but this information is REDUNDANT with what GNN message passing on the trimer already captures.
2. Random features match real features (52.11 vs 53.25) — the improvement in Iteration 1 was entirely due to pooling method artifact (global_add_pool vs global_mean_pool).
3. Chemistry weighting adds nothing (unweighted=51.89 vs weighted=53.25).
4. Graph-level feature injection (concatenation in prediction head) is ineffective — the GNN's trimer representation already encodes periodicity information.
5. Pure spectral MLP=76.71 confirms GNN structural information is essential.

**Root Cause Analysis**: The representation-usage gap cannot be solved by adding computed features to the prediction head. The GNN on the trimer graph already captures the structural information that spectral features encode through its 3-layer message passing. Adding spectral summaries as graph-level features is like telling the model something it already knows — redundant information that adds noise rather than signal. The 50→30 gap requires either:
(a) Node-level injection that affects message passing (not just prediction head) — atoms need periodicity-conditioned messages during MPNN
(b) Architecture that processes periodic topology differently (Chemprop directed bond messages)
(c) Pre-training mechanism that makes representations active conditioning signals (PGFT)

**MetaMethod Lessons**:
- Input-space injection at graph level is REDUNDANT with message passing on sufficiently large graphs (trimer with 3-layer GIN reaches all nodes)
- Random feature control is ESSENTIAL — without it, apparent improvements can be misattributed to physics content
- Pooling method artifacts can create false improvements (global_add_pool vs global_mean_pool)
- Correlation with target ≠ usefulness for model improvement — features can be correlated but redundant with existing model capacity

research_habits: **The proposed algorithm must be sufficiently innovative and original**, and the work of others must be properly cited.
Analyze why top models excel, maybe integrate their strengths to innovate, **copying is strictly prohibited.**
From Hypothesis to Experiment: Start with validated or pending hypotheses to design ingenious model structures and experimental strategies.
Match algorithms to physical reality: Consider the actual object behind the data. Models suited for crystals/alloys may not fit p-SMILES polymer datasets.
Negative results are valuable — BlochSpec failure (graph-level injection redundant) is as important as a positive result would be.
Simple baselines can be surprisingly strong — GIN+Trimer outperformed all 6 more complex combinations.
Small-Graph Paradox lesson: On graphs where MPNN already reaches all nodes, Transformer attention is redundant overhead.
Easy vs Hard Positive Pairs lesson: Contrastive learning needs HARD positives. Monomer-trimer pairs are EASY positives (cos_sim 0.94-0.97).
Architecture-Dependent Periodicity Encoding lesson: Periodic edges benefit Chemprop but hurt GIN.
Statistical Fluctuation Warning: Always verify promising results with multiple seeds before drawing conclusions.

Graph-Level Injection Redundancy lesson: Adding computed features at the graph level (concatenation in prediction head) is REDUNDANT with GNN message passing on sufficiently large graphs (trimer with 3-layer GIN reaches all nodes). The GNN already captures the structural information that spectral features encode. This was confirmed by: (a) random features matching real features, (b) unweighted matching weighted, (c) no statistical significance. The next approach must inject periodicity at the NODE level (during message passing) or change the message passing architecture itself.

Random Feature Control lesson: When adding extra features to a model, ALWAYS include a random feature control (same dimension, same distribution statistics, but random content). If random features match real features, the improvement comes from dimensionality/parameter count, not from the specific feature content. BlochSpec: random=52.11 vs real=53.25 — no difference.

Pooling Method Artifact lesson: global_add_pool vs global_mean_pool can create dramatic apparent improvements that are entirely artifacts. In BlochSpec Iteration 1, global_add_pool gave baseline=66.15 (vs reference 50.19 with global_mean_pool). Always verify that the baseline matches the reference before interpreting improvements.

Correlation ≠ Usefulness lesson: Features can have strong correlations with the target (low_freq_density r=-0.64 with Tg) but still be REDUNDANT with existing model capacity. The GNN on the trimer already captures what spectral features encode. Correlation with target does not guarantee that adding the feature improves model performance.
anti_self_deception: Zero Fabrication: Absolutely no hallucinations or fabrication of non-factual information.
The overfitting gap diagnostic: never celebrate lower train RMSE if test RMSE increases.
SSL Collapse Prevention lesson: JEPA-style EMA+MSE converges to trivial solution without VICReg.
Augmentation Difficulty Sweet Spot lesson: Too easy (cos_sim>0.93) = redundant. Too hard (cos_sim<0.80) = negative transfer.
Statistical Fluctuation Warning: Always verify with ≥3 seeds before claiming improvement.
Pre-training ≠ Better Representations: PI1M-scale PA contrastive pre-training reduces variance but does NOT improve mean.

Graph-Level Injection Redundancy: Computed features at prediction head level are redundant with GNN message passing. Random features match real features. Unweighted matches weighted. This is NOT a failure of the spectral features themselves (they have genuine Tg correlations) — it's a failure of the INJECTION MECHANISM. The features carry information that the model already has.

Three Exhausted Paradigms: (1) Contrastive pre-training (variance reduction only), (2) Architecture innovation on GIN family (50-54 ceiling), (3) Graph-level feature injection (redundant with message passing). Contrastive Difficulty Trap lesson: Easy positives provide redundant signal. Hard positives cause negative transfer. The simple GIN + contrastive paradigm is EXHAUSTED.
