This would be a major finding: changing HOW periodicity flows (via RU virtual nodes during MP) achieves what changing WHAT (features, prompts, pre-training) could not.", "If PolymerBipartite v2 achieves ~48-52 (only marginal improvement): Node-level periodicity injection via RU virtual nodes provides limited benefit. Possible reasons: (a) 3-layer GIN on trimer already reaches across RU boundaries, making RU-level aggregation redundant; (b) RU virtual nodes don't carry enough additional information beyond what atoms already compute. This would mean the 50→30 gap requires a fundamentally different architecture (Chemprop), not just adding structured virtual nodes to GIN.", "If PolymerBipartite v2 achieves >54 (worse than baseline): Adding RU virtual nodes increases overfitting despite controls. This would confirm that ANY virtual node addition to GIN is counterproductive on this dataset, and the gap requires switching to Chemprop entirely.", "If random RU control (ablation f) matches real RU (ablation b): RU nodes provide structural regularization (graph rewiring that alleviates over-squashing) but not discriminative periodicity information. The improvement comes from the BIPARTITE GRAPH TOPOLOGY (shorter commute paths), not from the RU node CONTENT. This partially validates LSR-MP's over-squashing analysis but weakens H8c (RU nodes don't need to be discriminative).", "If shuffled RU assignment (ablation g) performs significantly worse (~5+ RMSE points): The fixed atom-to-RU structural correspondence is essential. Randomly assigning atoms to RU nodes breaks the physical meaning of the bipartite structure. This validates that RU virtual nodes must aggregate PHYSICALLY MEANINGFUL groups of atoms (repeat units), not arbitrary clusters.", "If without RU→RU inter-coupling (ablation h) performs ~3-5 RMSE points worse: Inter-RU coupling at the RU level is essential for capturing chain-level periodicity. Without it, RU nodes only provide intra-RU summaries (similar to monomer encoder, risk of degeneracy). This validates that periodicity requires EXPLICIT inter-RU exchange, not just intra-RU aggregation.", "Progressive strategy: If PolymerBipartite v2 achieves ~42-48, the next step is to (a) combine with Chemprop backbone (Chemprop-Bipartite hybrid) for maximum architecture-periodicity compatibility, or (b) add PA contrastive pre-training on RU-level representations for additional periodicity priors."]}

memory.abstract: Chemprop-Polymer v2: Directed bond-level MPNN on periodic polymer graph with periodic edge feature engineering, bond message diagnostics, and architecture-contrastive hybrid path — refines mem_119 by adding (1) rich periodic edge bond features (backbone bond type, electronegativity gradient, RU boundary flag), (2) mandatory bond message cos_sim diagnostic for periodic edge messages, (3) explicit overfitting gap tracking and random periodic edge control, (4) progressive hybrid strategy combining Chemprop architecture with PolymerBipartite RU nodes
memory.keyword: Chemprop-Polymer v2, periodic edge features, bond message diagnostics, architecture-periodicity match, directed MPNN, overfitting control
memory.content:
{"H": ["H8e (Architecture-Periodicity Compatibility via Directed Bond Messages): The 50→30 gap requires matching the message-passing mechanism to the periodicity topology. Antoniuk et al. (mem_108) demonstrated that periodic edges benefit Chemprop (directed bond-level messages) but hurt GIN (atom-level sum-aggregation). Our Day 1 confirmed this: GIN+Cyclized=53.28 (worst). Chemprop processes BONDS as directed messages (each bond has separate forward h_{ij} and backward h_{ji} message vectors), allowing the periodic edge to carry specific inter-RU coupling information. In a polymer, the backbone bonds connecting one RU to the next are BOND-level phenomena: the chemistry of C-C vs C-O vs C-N backbone connections determines chain rigidity and Tg. Chemprop's directed messages naturally encode this — each periodic edge gets its own forward/reverse message vectors that can learn the specific chemistry of inter-RU coupling. GIN's atom-level aggregation treats the periodic edge as just another neighbor connection, creating a shortcut for memorization rather than a channel for periodicity propagation.", "H8f (Rich Periodic Edge Features Encode Inter-RU Chemistry): The periodic edge is not just a topological marker — it carries specific chemical information about the inter-RU connection. The bond type at the backbone boundary (single C-C, double C=C, aromatic, C-O, C-N, etc.) directly determines chain flexibility and Tg. Chemprop-Polymer v2 enriches the periodic edge bond features beyond the simple is_periodic flag in mem_119: (a) backbone_bond_type (same encoding as regular bonds: single=1, double=2, aromatic=3, triple=4), (b) electronegativity_gradient (|Δ electronegativity| between the two boundary atoms — captures bond polarity that affects inter-RU coupling), (c) boundary_atom_degree (degree of the boundary atoms in the infinite chain — captures branching complexity), (d) is_periodic flag (1 for periodic edge, 0 for regular bonds). These features give Chemprop's directed message passing explicit chemistry at the periodic boundary, enabling it to learn how different backbone types propagate information across RUs.", "H8g (Bond Message Diagnostics Validate Architecture-Periodicity Match): The key diagnostic for Chemprop-Polymer is whether the periodic edge bond messages are discriminative across polymers. After training, extract the forward message vector h_{ij}^{periodic} and reverse message vector h_{ji}^{periodic} for the periodic edge across all 7170 polymers. If these vectors show meaningful variation (different backbone types produce different periodic edge messages, cos_sim between different polymers' periodic edge messages < 0.90), Chemprop is USING the periodic edge to encode inter-RU coupling. If all periodic edge messages are near-identical (cos_sim > 0.95), the periodic edge is not being utilized — the architecture ignores the specific chemistry of the periodic connection. This diagnostic is analogous to PCFT's cos_sim diagnostic for monomer prompts, but applied at the bond message level where it matters for Chemprop."], "X": ["Chemprop-Polymer v2 Architecture:

(a) Polymer Graph Construction (same as Antoniuk et al.):
- For each p-SMILES, parse with RDKit, identify star atoms (*) and their bonding partners
- Construct TRIMER graph: concatenate 3 copies of the repeat unit, replace [*] with actual bonds to next RU
- Add PERIODIC EDGE: connect the terminal atoms (atoms that would bond to the 4th RU) with a special bond
- The periodic edge ensures all atoms have correct bonding environments and the representation is unique for different propagation sites

(b) Rich Periodic Edge Bond Features (increment over mem_119):
For each bond (including the periodic edge), compute the following features:
1. bond_type: {1: single, 2: double, 3: aromatic, 4: triple, 5: periodic_single, 6: periodic_double, 7: periodic_aromatic} — the periodic edge inherits the bond type of the backbone connection at the RU boundary
2. is_periodic: binary (1 for periodic edge, 0 for regular bonds)
3. electronegativity_gradient: |Δ electronegativity| between the two bonded atoms (Pauling scale) — for periodic edge, this captures the polarity of the inter-RU connection
4. boundary_atom_degree: degree of the higher-degree boundary atom in the infinite chain — captures branching complexity at the RU boundary
5. conjugated: binary (1 if bond is in a conjugated system)
6. in_ring: binary (1 if bond is in a ring)

For regular bonds: features 1,3,5,6 are standard RDKit bond features; is_periodic=0; boundary_atom_degree=0
For periodic edge: bond_type=5/6/7 (matching backbone chemistry); is_periodic=1; electronegativity_gradient and boundary_atom_degree computed from the boundary atoms

This gives Chemprop's directed message passing explicit chemistry at the periodic boundary, enabling it to learn how different backbone types propagate information across RUs.", "Chemprop MPNN Backbone (standard Chemprop with polymer graph):

- Use the official chemprop Python package (https://github.com/chemprop/chemprop)
- Initialize learned atom features (dim=hidden_dim) and bond features (dim=hidden_dim) from RDKit descriptors + periodic edge features
- 3 message-passing steps (T=3, as in Antoniuk et al.)
- Each step: for each directed bond (i→j), compute hidden bond message:
  h_{ij}^t = MLP_message(h_i^t, h_j^t, h_{ji}^{t-1}, f_{ij})
  where h_i, h_j are atom hidden states, h_{ji} is the reverse bond message, f_{ij} are bond features (including periodic edge features)
- After T steps, aggregate bond messages into atom hidden states:
  h_i = MLP_atom(h_i^0, Σ_{j∈neighbors(i)} h_{ji}^T)
- Global pooling: h_graph = mean_pool({h_i})
- Prediction: Tg = MLP_pred(h_graph) ∈ R

The PERIODIC EDGE is treated as a regular directed bond in Chemprop's message-passing: it gets its own forward h_{ij}^{periodic} and reverse h_{ji}^{periodic} message vectors, with bond features that encode the specific chemistry of the inter-RU connection. This allows Chemprop to learn how information propagates through the periodic boundary — the directed message structure ensures the periodic edge carries specific coupling information, not just a generic neighbor connection.", "Training Protocol:

- Dataset: 7170 Tg polymers, seed=71, 72/8/20 split, patience=30, best by val RMSE
- Use Chemprop's default hyperparameters as primary protocol (they are validated for this architecture):
  - hidden_dim=300 (Chemprop default, not 256 — architecture-specific)
  - depth=3 (message passing steps)
  - FFN hidden layers=2, FFN hidden dim=300
  - dropout=0.0 (Chemprop default)
  - LR=1e-4 (Chemprop default, different from our GIN protocol)
  - batch_size=50
  - epochs=100
- ALSO run with our GIN protocol for fair comparison (hidden_dim=256, LR=1e-3, batch_size=32)
- Multi-seed verification with ≥3 seeds (seeds {42, 71, 123}) — MANDATORY
- Memory estimate: Chemprop on trimer graphs (30-60 nodes, ~60-120 directed bonds including periodic edge) with hidden_dim=300. ~3-5MB per batch. Well within 11GB GPU.", "Key Ablations (all with multi-seed verification ≥3 seeds):

(a) Chemprop + monomer graph (no periodic edge, no trimer) — baseline for Chemprop architecture without periodicity encoding
(b) Chemprop + trimer graph (3 RUs, no periodic edge) — tests whether trimer representation helps with Chemprop (should, per Day 1 finding)
(c) Chemprop + polymer graph (trimer + periodic edge with rich features) — FULL MODEL, tests H8e+H8f+H8g
(d) Chemprop + polymer graph with MINIMAL periodic edge features (only is_periodic flag, no electronegativity_gradient or boundary_atom_degree) — tests H8f: whether rich periodic edge features are essential
(e) Chemprop + polymer graph with RANDOM periodic edge (connect random terminal atoms instead of correct ones) — tests whether the SPECIFIC chemistry of the periodic edge matters
(f) Chemprop + polymer graph with SHUFFLED periodic edge features (random values for electronegativity_gradient and boundary_atom_degree, correct is_periodic flag) — random feature control for periodic edge features
(g) GIN + trimer (Day 1 baseline = 50.19, mean_pool baseline = 52.46) — architecture comparison
(h) GIN + polymer graph (Day 1 GIN+Cyclized = 53.28) — architecture comparison: same periodicity encoding, different architecture (negative control)
(i) Chemprop + monomer + BlochSpec spectral features (concatenated in prediction head) — tests whether computed periodicity features help Chemprop (expected: YES, since Chemprop can USE periodicity through its architecture)
(j) Chemprop + polymer graph with PolymerBipartite RU virtual nodes (HYBRID: Chemprop backbone + RU-level bipartite message passing) — progressive strategy combining architecture-periodicity match with node-level periodicity injection"], "Mandatory Diagnostics:

1. Periodic Edge Bond Message Discriminability (cos_sim diagnostic):
   - After training, extract h_{ij}^{periodic} and h_{ji}^{periodic} for the periodic edge across ALL 7170 polymers
   - Compute pairwise cosine similarity between periodic edge message vectors across polymers
   - Expected: mean pairwise cos_sim < 0.90 (discriminative, unlike PCFT monomer cos_sim=0.963)
   - If cos_sim > 0.95: periodic edge messages are near-identical → Chemprop not utilizing the periodic edge's chemistry
   - Stratify by backbone type: compute cos_sim within C-C backbone polymers vs within C-O backbone polymers vs across backbone types
   - Expected: within-group cos_sim higher (~0.85), cross-group cos_sim lower (~0.70) → periodic edge messages encode backbone chemistry

2. Random Periodic Edge Control:
   - Ablation (e): connect random terminal atoms instead of the correct ones
   - If random periodic edge matches correct periodic edge: the SPECIFIC chemistry doesn't matter, just having an extra connection helps (topology effect, not chemistry effect)
   - If correct periodic edge significantly outperforms random: the specific inter-RU chemistry matters, validating H8f

3. Random Feature Control for Periodic Edge Features:
   - Ablation (f): random electronegativity_gradient and boundary_atom_degree values
   - If random features match real features: the rich periodic edge features are redundant with what Chemprop already learns from atom features
   - If real features significantly outperform random: the explicit chemistry encoding at the periodic edge provides genuinely new information

4. Overfitting Gap Analysis:
   - Compare train RMSE - test RMSE for all ablations
   - Expected: Chemprop overfitting gap < GIN overfitting gap (directed bond messages provide more structured information flow)
   - Track overfitting gap for Chemprop+monomer vs Chemprop+trimer vs Chemprop+polymer
   - If polymer graph increases overfitting gap: periodic edge enables memorization → need dropout or capacity reduction

5. Architecture Comparison:
   - Compare (c) Chemprop+polymer vs (g) GIN+trimer: same data (trimer), different architecture
   - Compare (c) Chemprop+polymer vs (h) GIN+polymer: same periodicity encoding, different architecture
   - The gap between (c) and (h) directly measures architecture-periodicity compatibility

6. Progressive Improvement Analysis:
   - Compare (a) monomer → (b) trimer → (c) polymer graph within Chemprop
   - Expected: monomer → trimer improvement ~2-4 RMSE (consistent with Day 1), trimer → polymer improvement ~2-4 RMSE (consistent with Antoniuk et al.'s ~4% finding)
   - Total expected: monomer → polymer ~4-8 RMSE improvement"], "Y": ["If H8e correct: Chemprop+polymer graph (ablation c) should significantly outperform GIN+polymer graph (ablation h, 53.28). Expected: Chemprop+polymer → ~42-48, GIN+polymer → ~53.28. The ~10-point gap validates that architecture-periodicity compatibility is critical — the same periodicity encoding (periodic edge) helps with Chemprop but hurts with GIN. This is the strongest validation of H8e.", "If H8f correct: Rich periodic edge features (ablation c) should outperform minimal periodic edge features (ablation d). Expected delta: ~1-3 RMSE points. The explicit chemistry encoding (backbone bond type, electronegativity gradient) at the periodic edge provides genuinely new information that Chemprop's directed messages can use. If minimal features match rich features: the periodic edge chemistry is already captured by atom features and bond type alone — explicit feature engineering is unnecessary.", "If H8g correct: Periodic edge bond message cos_sim should be <0.90 across polymers. Different backbone types (C-C, C-O, C-N) should produce different periodic edge message vectors. Within-group cos_sim should be ~0.80-0.85, cross-group cos_sim should be ~0.60-0.75. This validates that Chemprop's directed messages encode the specific chemistry of inter-RU coupling, not just a generic periodicity flag.", "Expected best result: ~42-48 RMSE with Chemprop+polymer graph (no pre-training). This closes 5-10 points of the 50→30 gap purely through architecture-periodicity matching, without any pre-training infrastructure. This is the SIMPLEST validated path.", "If Chemprop+polymer achieves ~38-42: Strong improvement (~10-14 points), approaching the range where combining with pre-training or PolymerBipartite RU nodes could approach SOTA. This validates H8e and makes Chemprop the preferred backbone for all future experiments.", "If Chemprop+polymer achieves ~48-50 (only marginal improvement over GIN+trimer=50.19): Architecture-periodicity compatibility helps but is not sufficient. The Tg dataset difficulty dominates. Possible reasons: (a) our Tg dataset is harder than Antoniuk et al.'s (their absolute RMSE was 37.35, suggesting easier dataset), (b) Chemprop's directed bond messages don't provide enough additional expressiveness for Tg prediction specifically.", "If Chemprop+polymer achieves >50 (no improvement over GIN+trimer): Chemprop doesn't help on our Tg dataset. This would be a surprising negative result given Antoniuk et al.'s literature evidence. Possible reasons: (a) dataset composition difference, (b) training protocol mismatch, (c) periodic edge construction errors.", "If random periodic edge (ablation e) performs similarly to correct periodic edge (~2 RMSE difference): The SPECIFIC chemistry of the periodic connection doesn't matter much — just having an extra connection helps Chemprop by increasing connectivity. This would partially weaken H8f but still validate H8e (Chemprop uses the extra connection effectively, unlike GIN which is hurt by it).", "If random periodic edge performs significantly worse (~5+ RMSE difference): The SPECIFIC chemistry of the inter-RU connection is essential. Chemprop's directed messages encode the backbone bond type at the periodic boundary, and random connections break this encoding. This strongly validates H8f.", "If Chemprop+monomer (ablation a) achieves ~48-52: Chemprop alone (without periodicity encoding) is comparable to GIN+trimer. The architecture itself doesn't provide a major advantage — the improvement comes from the COMBINATION of Chemprop architecture + periodic edge topology.", "If Chemprop+trimer (ablation b) achieves ~46-48: Trimer representation helps Chemprop (consistent with Day 1 finding), and the periodic edge provides additional ~2-4 RMSE improvement (consistent with Antoniuk et al.).", "If Chemprop+polymer+RU nodes (ablation j, hybrid) achieves ~35-40: Architecture-periodicity compatibility + node-level periodicity injection are COMPLEMENTARY. Chemprop provides the right architecture for directed bond messages on periodic edges; PolymerBipartite RU nodes provide additional inter-RU coupling at the node level. This combination could approach SOTA.", "Progressive strategy: If Chemprop+polymer achieves ~42-48, the next step is ablation (j) — adding PolymerBipartite RU virtual nodes on top of Chemprop backbone. This combines two mechanism changes: (1) directed bond messages on periodic edges (Chemprop), and (2) node-level periodicity injection via RU virtual nodes (PolymerBipartite). If both mechanism changes are complementary, this hybrid could approach ~35-40 RMSE."]}

memory.abstract: Conformer Entropy Landscape (CEL): Physics-first Tg prediction — compute conformational entropy from MMFF94 conformer energy landscapes of cyclized monomers via Adam-Gibbs-inspired formula, then correct systematic biases with kernel ridge regression on chemical descriptors, completely bypassing the exhausted GNN paradigm by reframing Tg prediction from a graph-property problem to a physics-computation + ML-correction problem
memory.keyword: conformer entropy landscape, Adam-Gibbs, physics-first, kernel correction, MMFF94, conformational entropy

H: H1 (Conformational Entropy Gap — the TRUE 50→30 source): The 50→30 RMSE gap exists because 2D graph neural networks CANNOT access the 3D conformational physics that fundamentally determines Tg. Per polymer physics (Adam-Gibbs theory), Tg ≈ T₂/(1 - Sc(Tg)/ΔCp), where Sc is the configurational entropy — the number of accessible chain conformations. Rigid polymers (aromatic backbones, few rotatable bonds) have low Sc → high Tg; flexible polymers (alkyl chains, many rotatable bonds) have high Sc → low Tg. This is a 3D physics quantity that depends on dihedral angle distributions, energy barriers between conformers, and inter-RU torsional coupling — NONE of which are captured by 2D graph topology. Every failed approach (contrastive, architecture innovation, feature injection) tried to make a 2D GNN learn this 3D physics implicitly. The gap persists because the information channel (2D graph → Tg) is fundamentally insufficient — it's like predicting protein folding from amino acid sequence without 3D structure. The solution is not to make the GNN more sophisticated; it's to COMPUTE the 3D physics directly and use ML only for correction.

H2 (Physics-First + ML-Correction Paradigm): Tg prediction should be reframed as a physics computation + ML bias correction problem, analogous to how weather prediction (Navier-Stokes + ML correction) and RadonPy (MD simulation + transfer learning correction) work. Step 1: COMPUTE a physics-informed Tg estimate from the conformer energy landscape (conformational entropy, energy range, backbone dihedral flexibility). Step 2: CORRECT the systematic bias of this physics estimate using kernel ridge regression (KRR) or Gaussian process regression (GPR) on chemical descriptors. The physics estimate captures the MAIN trend (backbone rigidity → Tg) through first-principles computation; ML only learns the RESIDUAL (force field limitations, missing inter-RU effects, secondary Tg determinants like polar interactions). This is a fundamentally simpler and more physically grounded learning problem than predicting Tg from scratch with a GNN.

H3 (PI1M Conformer Database Provides Mean-Level Training Data): Unlike contrastive pre-training on PI1M (which provided only variance reduction, not mean improvement — PerioGT-Lite FAILED), computing conformer landscapes for PI1M provides MEAN-LEVEL physics information about Tg trends across diverse polymer structures. For each of 1M polymers in PI1M, we can compute conformer landscape features (Sc_proxy, ΔE, backbone_flexibility) and a physics-informed Tg estimate Tg_phys. Even without experimental Tg labels, these physics-computed values provide a massive training signal for the correction model: the correction model can learn which chemical features cause MMFF94 to overestimate or underestimate Tg, using the physics-computed values as pseudo-labels. This is transfer learning from physics computation to experimental data, exactly analogous to RadonPy's approach (MD-computed properties → transfer learning → experimental correction).
X:
Phase 1: Conformer Landscape Computation (for all 7170 Tg polymers)

For each p-SMILES in the Tg dataset:
1. Cyclize the monomer: connect the two star-bonded atoms with a bond, creating a ring that represents the periodic chain topology. This ensures all atoms have correct bonding environments (same as the cyclized representation from Day 1, but used for 3D conformer generation, not as a 2D graph input).
2. Generate N=50 conformers using RDKit ETKDG v3 (extended stochastic sampling with torsional preferences). ETKDG is fast (~0.01s per molecule) and produces diverse conformers covering the energy landscape.
3. Optimize each conformer with MMFF94 (max 2000 iterations, convergence threshold 0.01 kcal/mol/Å). This provides relative energies E_i for each conformer.
4. Compute pairwise RMSD matrix between all conformers (50×50 matrix per polymer).
5. Cluster conformers by RMSD (threshold 0.5Å) to identify distinct conformational states → N_clusters.
6. Extract backbone dihedral angles for each conformer: identify backbone dihedrals (atoms in the main chain path between the two star-bonded positions), compute their values across all conformers.

Total compute time: ~2-3 hours for 7170 polymers on a single CPU (RDKit is CPU-based, no GPU needed). This is extremely efficient compared to MD simulations (RadonPy takes hours per polymer).

Phase 2: Conformer Landscape Feature Extraction

For each polymer, extract the following physics-derived features from the conformer landscape:

(a) Conformational entropy proxy: Sc_proxy = ln(N_clusters / N_total). Normalized by total conformer count to control for generation randomness. N_clusters captures the number of DISTINCT conformational states — rigid polymers have few clusters (low Sc_proxy), flexible polymers have many (high Sc_proxy).

(b) Energy landscape shape: ΔE = E_max - E_min (energy range), E_std = std(E_i) (energy diversity), E_skew = skewness of energy distribution (asymmetric landscapes indicate dominant low-energy conformers). These capture how easily the chain can transition between conformations — high ΔE means large energy barriers between states.

(c) Backbone dihedral flexibility: For each backbone dihedral, compute std(dihedral_values) across conformers. Average across all backbone dihedrals → mean_backbone_flexibility. High flexibility = many accessible dihedral states = low Tg. Also compute: fraction_of_backbone_dihedrals_with_std > 30° (highly flexible dihedrals), and fraction_with_std < 10° (rigid dihedrals).

(d) Conformer geometry diversity: mean pairwise RMSD across all conformers (how different are the conformers from each other), max pairwise RMSD (extreme conformational range), RMSD to lowest-energy conformer (how far are other conformers from the ground state).

(e) Inter-RU coupling features: For the cyclized monomer, the bond connecting the two star-bonded atoms is the inter-RU connection. Compute the dihedral angle distribution at this junction across conformers → junction_flexibility. This captures how the repeat unit connects to its neighbors in the chain — the key inter-RU coupling that H6 identified as essential.

(f) KME descriptor of conformer energy distribution: Apply kernel mean embedding (mem_063) to the distribution of conformer energies. Use Gaussian RBF kernel k(E, E') = exp(-||E-E'||²/2σ²), discretize at d=10 grid points over [E_min, E_max]. This preserves the FULL distributional shape of the energy landscape (multimodal energy distributions indicate distinct conformational basins), unlike summary statistics (mean, std) that lose this information.

Phase 3: Physics-Informed Tg Estimate (Adam-Gibbs-inspired)

Compute a physics-informed Tg estimate using the conformer landscape features:

Tg_phys = w₁ · (1/Sc_proxy) + w₂ · ΔE + w₃ · mean_backbone_flexibility + w₄ · junction_flexibility + w₀

Where weights w₀...w₄ are fitted by LINEAR REGRESSION on the training set (5164 polymers). This is NOT a neural network — it's a simple physics-informed linear model that captures the main trend:
- 1/Sc_proxy: inverse conformational entropy (Adam-Gibbs: Tg ∝ 1/Sc)
- ΔE: energy range (larger barriers → higher Tg)
- mean_backbone_flexibility: flexible backbones → lower Tg
- junction_flexibility: flexible inter-RU connections → lower Tg

Expected performance of Tg_phys alone: ~55-65 RMSE (captures main trend but has systematic biases from MMFF94 limitations, missing inter-RU effects beyond single RU, and missing secondary Tg determinants). This is worse than GNN baseline (50.19) but provides a PHYSICS-GROUNDED starting point that ML can improve.

Phase 4: ML Bias Correction (the key innovation)

Train a correction model on the RESIDUAL: Tg_residual = Tg_true - Tg_phys

The correction model uses TWO types of input features:

1. Chemical descriptors (2D): 200 RDKit descriptors + 1024-bit ECFP6 fingerprints from the monomer SMILES. These capture chemical features that MMFF94 misses (polar interactions, hydrogen bonding, aromatic stacking, side group effects).

2. Conformer landscape KME descriptors (3D): The kernel mean embedding of the conformer energy distribution (from Phase 2f). This preserves the full energy landscape shape that simple linear regression on Sc_proxy/ΔE cannot capture.

Correction model options (test all three):
(a) Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) with RBF kernel on combined features — simplest, most robust, well-validated for materials property prediction (mem_063, mem_031). Hyperparameters: kernel bandwidth σ, regularization λ. Optimize via grid search on validation set.
(b) Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) with RBF kernel — provides uncertainty estimates, naturally handles small datasets. Same hyperparameters as KRR.
(c) Shallow MLP (2 hidden layers, 128 neurons each, ReLU) on combined features — more expressive but higher overfitting risk. Use dropout=0.3, L2 regularization.

Final prediction: Tg_final = Tg_phys + Tg_ML_correction

Training protocol: seed=71, 72/8/20 split, patience=30, best by val RMSE. For KRR/GPR: 5-fold CV for hyperparameter tuning. For MLP: Adam optimizer, LR=1e-3, cosine annealing.

Phase 5: PI1M-Scale Pre-training for Correction Model (transfer learning from physics computation)

Compute conformer landscapes for 100K-300K polymers from PI1M (CPU-based, ~30-90 minutes total):
1. For each PI1M polymer, generate 50 conformers, compute landscape features, compute Tg_phys estimate using the SAME weights w₀...w₄ fitted from Tg training set.
2. Use Tg_phys as pseudo-labels for PI1M polymers (no experimental Tg available, but physics-computed estimates provide training signal).
3. Pre-train the correction model on PI1M: learn to predict Tg_residual_pi1m = 0 (the correction should be zero for physics-computed values, since there's no experimental bias to correct). This teaches the model that the physics estimate is approximately correct, and the correction should be small.
4. Fine-tune on Tg dataset: learn the actual systematic biases of MMFF94 against experimental Tg values.

This is DIFFERENT from contrastive pre-training (which failed): instead of learning embedding invariances, we're learning that physics-computed Tg estimates are approximately correct and only need small corrections. The pre-training signal is MEAN-LEVEL (physics-computed Tg values), not VARIANCE-LEVEL (embedding invariances).

Phase 6: Hybrid GNN + Conformer Approach (optional, if pure physics+ML doesn't close the gap)

If the pure physics+ML approach achieves ~40-45 RMSE (significant improvement but not full gap closure), combine with GNN:

(a) Use conformer landscape features as NODE FEATURES in the GNN (not graph-level features). For each atom in the trimer graph, compute its local conformer contribution: the dihedral angles involving this atom across conformers, the energy contribution of this atom's bonds, the flexibility of bonds connected to this atom. These are 3D physics-derived node features that the 2D GNN genuinely cannot capture through topology alone.

(b) This is NODE-LEVEL injection of 3D physics during message passing — different from graph-level injection (BlochSpec, which was redundant). Node-level injection changes HOW information flows through the model: atoms with high local flexibility send different messages than atoms with low flexibility, and this information propagates through the same channels as atomic features.

(c) CRITICAL: include random conformer feature control. Generate random features with the same dimensionality and distribution statistics as the real conformer features, but with random content. If random features match real features, the conformer information is redundant with what the GNN already captures from 2D topology. If real features significantly outperform random, the 3D physics information provides genuinely new information.

Key Ablations (all with multi-seed verification ≥3 seeds):

(a) Tg_phys alone (linear regression on conformer landscape features, no ML correction) — tests H1: whether conformational entropy captures the main Tg trend. Expected: ~55-65 RMSE.
(b) KRR on chemical descriptors only (no conformer features, no physics estimate) — baseline for descriptor-based ML. Expected: ~45-50 RMSE (descriptor methods typically perform comparably to GNN on polymers, per mem_033, mem_071).
(c) Tg_phys + KRR correction on chemical descriptors — tests H2: whether physics-first + ML correction improves over pure ML. Expected: ~35-42 RMSE.
(d) Tg_phys + KRR correction on chemical + conformer KME descriptors — FULL MODEL, tests H1+H2. Expected: ~32-38 RMSE.
(e) Tg_phys + KRR correction with PI1M pre-training — tests H3: whether physics-computed pre-training provides mean-level improvement. Expected: ~30-35 RMSE.
(f) Pure GNN baseline (GIN+Trimer=50.19) — architecture comparison.
(g) Tg_phys + MLP correction (shallow neural network) — tests whether more expressive correction model helps.
(h) Tg_phys + GPR correction — tests whether uncertainty-aware correction helps.
(i) Random conformer feature control: replace real conformer features with random features (same dimension, same distribution statistics). If random matches real → conformer features are redundant. If real outperforms random → 3D physics provides genuinely new information.
(j) Tg_phys computed from dimer conformers (instead of cyclized monomer) — tests whether inter-RU conformer information improves the physics estimate.
(k) Tg_phys computed from trimer conformers — tests whether longer chain conformers improve the physics estimate.
(l) GNN + conformer node features (Phase 6 hybrid) — tests whether node-level 3D physics injection helps the GNN.
Y: If H1 correct: Tg_phys alone (ablation a) should show strong correlation with experimental Tg (R² > 0.5, RMSE ~55-65). The conformational entropy proxy (1/Sc_proxy) should be the single strongest predictor, with correlation r > -0.6 with Tg (inverse relationship: high Sc → low Tg). The backbone dihedral flexibility should also show strong correlation (r < -0.5). If Tg_phys has R² < 0.3 or RMSE > 70: MMFF94 conformer landscapes don't capture Tg-relevant physics — the force field is too inaccurate or the cyclized monomer doesn't represent chain conformations well.

If H2 correct: Tg_phys + KRR correction (ablation c) should significantly outperform pure KRR on chemical descriptors (ablation b). Expected: physics+ML → ~35-42 RMSE, pure ML → ~45-50 RMSE. The ~10-15 point improvement validates that the physics estimate captures the main trend and ML only needs to learn the residual — a much simpler problem than learning Tg from scratch. If physics+ML matches pure ML (~45-50): the physics estimate doesn't provide useful information beyond what chemical descriptors already capture. This would mean MMFF94 conformer landscapes are too noisy to be helpful.

If H3 correct: PI1M pre-trained correction model (ablation e) should outperform correction model trained only on Tg dataset (ablation d). Expected: pre-trained → ~30-35 RMSE, no pre-training → ~35-38 RMSE. The ~3-5 point improvement validates that physics-computed pre-training provides MEAN-LEVEL training signal (unlike contrastive pre-training which provided only variance reduction). If pre-training doesn't help: the physics-computed pseudo-labels are too noisy for useful pre-training, or the correction model is too simple to benefit from pre-training.

Expected best result: ~30-35 RMSE with Tg_phys + KRR correction on chemical + conformer KME descriptors + PI1M pre-training. This closes most or all of the 50→30 gap through a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT PARADIGM (physics computation + ML correction) rather than GNN architecture/pre-training innovation. If this achieves ~30.8 or better: the physics-first paradigm is superior to the GNN paradigm for polymer Tg prediction — a major paradigm shift result.

If the full model achieves ~35-40 RMSE: significant improvement (10-15 points over GNN baseline) but gap to SOTA remains. The remaining gap may require: (a) better force fields (OA force field, DFT-optimized conformers for a subset), (b) longer chain conformers (dimer/trimer landscapes), (c) more sophisticated correction models (GPR with custom kernels), or (d) hybrid GNN + conformer node features (Phase 6).

If random conformer feature control (ablation i) shows real features significantly outperforming random (~5+ RMSE difference): 3D conformer physics provides genuinely NEW information that 2D chemical descriptors cannot capture. This validates H1 — the conformational entropy gap is real and 3D physics is the missing information channel. This would be the most important diagnostic result, proving that the 50→30 gap is fundamentally an information gap (2D → 3D), not an architecture gap.

If random conformer features match real features: conformer landscape information is already captured by 2D chemical descriptors (rotatable bond fraction, aromatic content, etc.). This would weaken H1 but not invalidate the approach — the physics-first paradigm may still help by providing a better starting point (Tg_phys) for ML correction, even if the conformer features themselves are redundant with 2D descriptors.

If dimer/trimer conformer landscapes (ablations j, k) significantly outperform cyclized monomer landscapes (~5+ RMSE improvement): inter-RU conformer information is essential. The cyclized monomer captures intra-RU conformations but misses inter-RU dihedral coupling. This validates H6 (periodicity is inter-RU) from a 3D physics perspective — the conformer landscape must include inter-RU geometry to capture Tg-relevant physics.

If GNN + conformer node features (ablation l) achieves ~35-40 RMSE: node-level 3D physics injection helps the GNN, confirming that the information gap (2D → 3D) can also be bridged by enriching node features with physics-derived 3D information. This provides a second path forward: instead of abandoning GNN entirely, inject 3D physics at the node level during message passing. This is different from graph-level injection (BlochSpec failed) because node-level features change HOW atoms communicate during MP.

Diagnostic: Correlation analysis between conformer landscape features and Tg:
- Sc_proxy vs Tg: expected r < -0.6 (inverse: more conformations → lower Tg)
- ΔE vs Tg: expected r > 0.4 (larger energy range → higher Tg)
- mean_backbone_flexibility vs Tg: expected r < -0.5 (flexible backbone → lower Tg)
- junction_flexibility vs Tg: expected r < -0.3 (flexible inter-RU connection → lower Tg)
If these correlations are weak (|r| < 0.3): MMFF94 conformer landscapes don't capture Tg-relevant physics. Need better force field or different conformer generation strategy.

Diagnostic: Compare Tg_phys residual distribution:
- If Tg_residual = Tg_true - Tg_phys has mean ≈ 0 and std ≈ 30-40: the physics estimate captures the main trend well, and the residual is small enough for ML correction to handle.
- If Tg_residual has systematic bias (mean ≠ 0, e.g., MMFF94 consistently overestimates Tg by 20K): the correction model can learn this systematic bias easily.
- If Tg_residual has std > 60: the physics estimate is too noisy for useful correction. Need better physics computation.

Overfitting diagnostic: KRR/GPR should have minimal overfitting (kernel methods are well-regularized). MLP correction may overfit — compare train vs test RMSE for MLP. If MLP overfitting gap > 10: use KRR/GPR instead. The physics-first paradigm should have LOWER overfitting risk than pure GNN because: (a) the main prediction is physics-computed (no learning needed), (b) the correction model only learns residuals (simpler problem), (c) kernel methods are inherently well-regularized.

Progressive improvement analysis:
- Tg_phys alone → Tg_phys + KRR on chemical descriptors → Tg_phys + KRR on chemical + conformer descriptors → + PI1M pre-training
- Each step should add ~5-10 RMSE points of improvement
- If improvement is monotonic: the physics-first paradigm is systematically better with more information
- If improvement plateaus early: the physics estimate ceiling limits further improvement

memory.abstract: HSG generalizes the virtual node concept through recursive graph coarsening, creating hierarchical support structures that enhance long-range information exchange in MPNNs without custom layers, achieving SOTA on PascalVOC-SP and Peptides-struct while showing that on small graphs a single VN suffices.

content.background: Message-Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) are widely used for graph learning but suffer from limited receptive fields — information exchange is confined to neighboring nodes each round, creating bottlenecks for long-range dependencies. Several strategies address this: graph rewiring (adding/removing edges), virtual nodes (VN connecting to all nodes for global exchange), and Graph Transformers (GTs with full attention). VNs have shown promise but provide only a single global bottleneck node. GTs eliminate locality constraints but have prohibitive asymptotic complexity for large graphs. Prior work on VNs (Rosenbluth et al., 2024; Southern et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2023) uses separate update steps for the VN, requiring custom layers. Graph coarsening has been used for scalability of GTs (Zhang et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023) or for graph classification (Ying et al., 2019), but not specifically to improve long-range information exchange in MPNNs. The motivation for HSG is to generalize VNs into multi-level hierarchical support structures that provide richer pathways for information flow while maintaining computational efficiency and requiring no custom MP layers — the HSG nodes and edges participate in standard message-passing as regular graph elements.
content.method:
The core idea of Hierarchical Support Graphs (HSGs) is to recursively coarsen the original graph, creating a hierarchy of increasingly coarse support graphs (super-nodes representing clusters, super-edges representing inter-cluster connections), then integrate all layers back into the original graph as regular nodes and edges for standard message-passing.

**Construction Procedure**: (1) Apply a coarsening algorithm (e.g., METIS partitioning) to the input graph G, creating k node clusters that minimize inter-cluster edges with similar cluster sizes. Contract clusters to super-nodes and inter-cluster edges to super-edges, yielding the first support graph H^(1). (2) Recursively repeat Z-1 more times: H^(i+1) = f_r(H^(i)), where f_r is the coarsening function with ratio r (fraction of nodes retained). (3) Connect each node to its direct super-node via vertical edges. (4) The augmented graph G^H contains all original nodes/edges, all horizontal edges within each support layer, and all vertical edges connecting nodes to their super-nodes.

**Theoretical Properties**: Theorem 3 shows total nodes in G^H are bounded by n/(1-r), diameter by 2·log(n)/(-log(r)), and edges by O(m·log(n)/(-log(r))). Theorem 4 establishes that to preserve average node degree, the coarsening must satisfy r(i) = Ω(n/m) and C(i) = Θ(R(i)), where C(i) is cumulative edge reduction and R(i) is cumulative node reduction. Theorems 5-6 analyze random coarsening on Erdős-Rényi graphs, showing node degree preservation up to constant factors for p(n) = Θ(n^{-β}) with β ∈ [0, 1/2] ∪ [1, ∞).

**Integration into MPNNs**: HSG nodes/edges are treated as regular graph elements in standard message-passing — no custom update steps needed. This is a key design choice distinguishing HSG from prior VN work (Rosenbluth et al., 2024) which uses separate VN update steps. Super-node features are imputed (mean of children for vision datasets, mode for molecule datasets) or set to dummy embeddings indicating hierarchical position. Super-edge features similarly use imputed or dummy embeddings. The dummy embeddings are especially important for GatedGCN which uses edge-gating to distinguish neighbor types.

**Adapted Graph Pooling**: For graph-level tasks, instead of global pooling over all original nodes, pool only over the highest HSG layer H^(Z) nodes. This works because information from all original nodes must travel through the hierarchical structure to reach the top layer, creating a natural aggregated representation.

**Why this design works**: (1) Multi-level hierarchy provides multiple pathways for long-range information exchange, unlike a single VN bottleneck. (2) METIS coarsening preserves graph structural properties (minimizing inter-cluster edges), maintaining meaningful connectivity patterns. (3) Vertical edges create shortcuts proportional to log(n) diameter, enabling information to traverse the graph in fewer MP rounds. (4) The approach adds only O(n/(1-r)) nodes and O(m·log(n)/(-log(r))) edges — small overhead compared to GTs. (5) No custom layers means the method is agnostic to the specific MPNN architecture used.
content.experiment:
**Datasets**: PascalVOC-SP, COCO-SP (vision superpixel datasets from LRGB), Peptides-func, Peptides-struct (molecule datasets from LRGB), ogbg-molpcba (molecule dataset from OGB). Models constrained to <500K parameters on LRGB, unconstrained on ogbg-molpcba.

**Baselines**: GCN, GatedGCN, SAN, GPS, GRIT, DRew, S²GCN, GCN-VN, GatedGCN-VN (from Rosenbluth et al., 2024). 4 runs on LRGB datasets, 7 runs on ogbg-molpcba.

**Topology Analysis (Table 1)**: On 100 random Peptides-func graphs, HSG augmentation (METIS (0.25,·)) reduces diameter from 57 to 4, avg shortest path from 20.90 to 3.81, expected effective resistance from 20.24 to 1.44, expected commute time from 7740 to 1112, and increases average node connectivity (ANC) from 1.02 to 2.28. VN reduces these measures even further (diameter=2, resistance=0.90) but has lower ANC (2.02). Random coarsening has lower resistance/commute time and higher ANC than METIS, but worse predictive performance — indicating preserved graph structure matters.

**Main Results (Table 2)**: GatedGCN-HSG achieves SOTA on PascalVOC-SP (46.04 F1) and Peptides-struct (24.21 MAE). Outperforms GatedGCN-VN on PascalVOC-SP (46.04 vs 44.77), COCO-SP (35.35 vs 32.44), Peptides-struct (24.21 vs 24.75). On Peptides-func, GatedGCN-HSG (68.66) slightly underperforms GatedGCN-VN (68.23) and S²GCN (73.11). GCN-HSG underperforms GCN-VN on vision datasets — attributed to GCN lacking edge-gating mechanism to distinguish HSG nodes/edges.

**Ablation — Coarsening Configurations (Table 3)**: On Peptides-func with GCN-HSG, METIS (0.5,·) achieves 68.91, METIS (0.25,·) 68.71, Random (0.25,·) 67.39, Random (0.5,·) 67.92, VN (·) 68.19. METIS consistently outperforms random coarsening despite random having better topology measures — structure preservation is important. VN integrated into standard MP performs comparably to smaller METIS HSGs.

**Ablation — Feature Imputation (Table 4)**: On PascalVOC-SP (GatedGCN-HSG), imputed-node + dummy-edge achieves best (46.04). Dummy edges help GatedGCN's edge-gating distinguish real vs hierarchical edges. On Peptides-func (GCN-HSG), dummy-node configurations outperform imputed-node (68.91 vs 66.31), since GCN cannot use edge features and needs clear hierarchical node markers.

**Ablation — Prediction Head (Table 5)**: On graph-level tasks, top-layer pooling significantly outperforms global pooling for Peptides-struct (24.21 vs 24.75) and ogbg-molpcba (31.29 vs 30.14), but global pooling is better for Peptides-func (68.91 vs 67.30). The difference: Peptides-struct and ogbg-molpcba use only a single VN as HSG (small graphs), so all global information must pass through it, making top-layer pooling natural. Peptides-func uses a 2-layer HSG where information can also flow through lower layers.

**Key Configuration Details**: ogbg-molpcba and Peptides-struct use coarsening (·) — just a single VN. PascalVOC-SP and COCO-SP use (0.05,·) — one hierarchical layer then VN. Peptides-func uses (0.5,·) — coarsen to 50% then VN.
content.result:
HSG achieves state-of-the-art on PascalVOC-SP (46.04 F1) and Peptides-struct (24.21 MAE), outperforming single VN methods and matching/exceeding Graph Transformers on several datasets. The key performance principles: (1) Multi-level hierarchy provides richer information pathways than a single VN bottleneck, improving ANC from 1.02 to 2.28. (2) METIS coarsening preserves graph structure, which is critical — random coarsening has better topology measures but worse performance. (3) Edge-gating mechanisms (GatedGCN) are essential for distinguishing HSG elements; GCN without gating underperforms VN baselines on vision datasets. (4) On small graphs (ogbg-molpcba avg 26 nodes), a single VN suffices — larger HSGs are unnecessary. (5) Top-layer pooling works better than global pooling when all information must flow through the hierarchy apex.

**Limitations**: (1) GCN-based models struggle without edge-gating to distinguish HSG nodes/edges, limiting applicability to simple MPNNs. (2) On small graphs, HSG provides no advantage over a single VN — the hierarchical structure is only beneficial for larger graphs. (3) The coarsening is pre-computed and fixed — no learned/adaptive coarsening. (4) Feature imputation strategy (mean/mode vs dummy) is dataset-dependent and requires tuning.

**Relevance to polymer research**: Polymer trimer graphs (30-60 nodes) are small like ogbg-molpcba (avg 26), where HSG paper shows a single VN works best. This confirms the Small-Graph Paradox from MetaMethod — on small graphs where MPNN already reaches all nodes, hierarchical augmentation provides limited benefit. However, the HSG concept of structure-preserving coarsening (METIS) and the principle that edge-gating helps distinguish virtual elements are transferable insights. The top-layer pooling idea could benefit Tg prediction if RU virtual nodes are used.
content.dataset: PascalVOC-SP, COCO-SP, Peptides-func, Peptides-struct (LRGB), ogbg-molpcba (OGB)
content.topic_relation: Directly relates to H5 (Architecture-Periodicity Matching) and H8 (Message-Passing Mechanism Change). HSG is a VN generalization — Day 1 experiments showed GIN+VN increased overfitting (53.78 vs 50.19 baseline). The paper confirms that on small graphs (avg 26 nodes), a single VN suffices and larger HSGs are unnecessary, aligning with the Small-Graph Paradox. The finding that GCN without edge-gating cannot distinguish HSG elements explains why GIN+VN failed — GIN has no mechanism to gate/distinguish virtual node messages from real node messages, causing overfitting. The METIS-vs-random coarsening result (structure preservation matters) supports the principle that periodicity encoding must preserve meaningful structure, not just add random shortcuts.
content.topic_contribution: Three actionable insights: (1) **Edge-gating is essential for VN/HSG success** — GatedGCN-HSG outperforms GatedGCN-VN, but GCN-HSG underperforms GCN-VN. This explains Day 1 GIN+VN failure: GIN has no edge-gating, so VN messages flood all nodes indiscriminately, causing overfitting. For PolymerBipartite (H8 candidate), the RU virtual node MUST have a gating/attention mechanism to distinguish periodicity-carrying messages from regular atom messages. (2) **On small graphs, single VN suffices** — polymer trimers (30-60 nodes) are in the regime where HSG hierarchy adds no benefit over a single VN. This means PolymerBipartite should use a single RU virtual node per repeat unit, not a multi-level hierarchy. (3) **Top-layer pooling for graph-level tasks** — if using RU virtual nodes, pool only over RU nodes for Tg prediction instead of global pooling over all atoms. This could reduce noise from atom-level representations that are less relevant to the periodic property.

memory.abstract: XIMP introduces cross-graph inter-message passing that performs message passing both within and across multiple related graph representations (molecular graph + junction tree + extended reduced graph), supporting direct and indirect communication between abstractions, strictly generalizing HIMP and improving expressivity beyond 1-WL.

content.background: Molecular property prediction is central to drug discovery, but GNNs often underperform in data-scarce regimes and fail to surpass traditional fingerprint methods (ECFP). Standard message-passing GNNs are limited by the 1-WL test, failing to distinguish certain molecular structures (e.g., decalin vs. bicyclopentyl, small-cycle detection). Prior remedies include higher-order WL extensions and invariant graph networks, but these are computationally demanding. A lightweight approach is to combine graph models: HIMP couples the molecular graph with a junction tree (JT) abstraction, enabling inter-message passing (IMP) that exceeds 1-WL expressivity. However, prior work either (i) processes abstractions sequentially (RG-MPNN), (ii) restricts message passing to local aggregation within each graph with super-node pooling (RelMole), (iii) communicates only indirectly via the molecular graph (Neural Atoms), or (iv) uses only a single abstraction (HIMP, Wollschläger et al.). No prior method fully exploits inter-graph communication across multiple chemically interpretable abstractions. The key motivation: simultaneously using multiple alternative graph models (molecular graph, JT, extended reduced graph/ErG) can introduce suitable inductive bias, improving sample efficiency and predictive performance, especially in low-data regimes where GNNs typically fail to surpass fingerprints.
content.method: XIMP performs message passing iteratively within and across an arbitrary number of related graph representations. For cheminformatics, it combines three views: (1) the molecular graph G (atoms as nodes, bonds as edges), (2) the junction tree T_JT (decomposes molecules into overlapping fragments — rings and bridges — organized as a tree, capturing hierarchical fragment organization and coarse-grained connectivity), and (3) the extended reduced graph T_ErG (encodes pharmacophoric features — H-bond donors/acceptors, aromatic rings, hydrophobic groups, charges — and atom-level topological relationships relevant to biological activity, providing fine-grained pharmacophoric information absent in JTs and molecular graphs). Node correspondence matrices S_i ∈ {0,1}^{|V(G)|×|V(T_i)|} link the molecular graph to each reduced graph, where S_i[u,v]=1 indicates atom u belongs to reduced node v. These matrices naturally handle overlapping abstractions (fused rings, functional groups where one atom maps to multiple reduced nodes). XIMP introduces two inter-message passing mechanisms: (1) Indirect Inter-Message Passing (I²MP): exchanges information between G and each T_i within each layer. Messages from T_i to G: X_i^(l) = σ(̃S_i · T_i^(l-1) · W_{i,1}^(l)), where ̃S_i = D^{-1}S_i is the row-normalized correspondence matrix. Messages from G to T_i: M_i^(l) = σ(̃S_i^⊤ · X^(l-1) · W_{i,2}^(l)). Stacking layers enables indirect communication between reduced graphs via G. (2) Direct Inter-Message Passing (DIMP): allows direct communication between pairs of reduced graphs T_k → T_i via M_{k→i}^(l) = σ(̃S_{ik} · T_k^(l-1) · W_{k→i}^(l)), where ̃S_{ik} = D_{T,i}^{-1} · S_i^⊤ · D_{G,k}^{-1} · S_k. The normalization prevents multiplicity-induced overweighting: D_{G,k}^{-1} splits each atom's contribution evenly across its T_k memberships, while D_{T,i}^{-1} averages per-atom signals over atoms summarized by each T_i node. Proposition 3.1 proves ̃S_{ik} is row-stochastic (each row sums to 1), bounding message magnitudes and preserving constant embeddings. The overall layer update combines standard within-graph MP with inter-graph messages: X^(l) = 𝔛^(l) + Σ_i X_i^(l) (molecular graph gets contributions from all abstractions), T_i^(l) = 𝔗_i^(l) + M_i^(l) + Σ_{k≠i} M_{k→i}^(l) (each abstraction gets contributions from molecular graph AND other abstractions). All terms are computed from the previous layer's embeddings, ensuring uniform receptive field expansion. The READOUT function is a learnable combination of mean pooling across all graph representations: h_G = mean(X^(L))·W_0 ⊕_j mean(T_j^(L))·W_j. Expressivity: Theorem 3.2 proves HIMP's hypothesis class is strictly contained in XIMP's (ℋ_HIMP(L,d) ⊆ ℋ_XIMP(L,d,n)). Proposition 3.3 shows that two molecules indistinguishable by 1-WL on each individual graph (G, JT, ErG) become distinguishable on the compound graph 𝒢(G;T,R) with inter-graph edges — demonstrating that cross-abstraction communication creates new discriminative power beyond any single view. Complexity: per-layer runtime scales linearly with graph size but quadratically in hidden dimension d and number of abstractions n; with n≤2 in practice, this is a modest constant-factor increase over HIMP.
content.experiment: Datasets: 10 diverse molecular property prediction tasks from MoleculeNet (ESOL solubility: 1128 molecules, FreeSolv hydration free energy: 642, Lipo lipophilicity: 4200) and Polaris (ADMET: HLM/MLM/KSOL/LogD/MDR1-MDCKII, each 560 molecules; Potency: MERS-CoV-Mpro and SARS-CoV-2-Mpro pIC50, each 1328). Baselines: ECFP (fixed fingerprint, only regression head trained), GCN, GIN, GAT, GraphSAGE (best-performing per task shown as 'GNN'), and HIMP. Training: Adam optimizer, MAE loss, stratified 10-fold cross-validation on binned targets for hyperparameter selection, 10% scaffold-split test set for final evaluation. Hyperparameter grid: MP layers (1/2/3), hidden dim (16/32), output dim (16/32), batch size (64/128), regression head dim (16/32), epochs (50/100/150). XIMP-specific: graph abstraction selection (ErG vs JT), message-passing scheme (I²MP vs DIMP vs both), JT resolution (1-3), reduced graph embedding dim (16/32). Approximately 1M training runs total. Two evaluation protocols: (1) Table 1 — test MAE for hyperparameters chosen by lowest mean validation MAE (conservative, realistic); (2) Table 2 — test MAE for best hyperparameters per dataset (optimistic upper bound). Ablation: XIMP variants (a) I²MP+MP, (b) DIMP+MP, (c) MP only with late fusion, (d) DIMP+I²MP+MP; JT resolution 1-3 with different MP schemes; ErG vs JT vs both combinations.
content.result: XIMP achieves best or second-best performance across most tasks. With validation-selected hyperparameters (Table 1): XIMP best in 4/10 tasks, HIMP best in 4/10, but XIMP's performance profile (ECDF) dominates all baselines across all tasks, indicating superior robustness. With best-per-dataset hyperparameters (Table 2): XIMP best in 6/10 tasks, including 4/5 ADMET tasks. XIMP particularly excels on ADMET tasks leveraging pharmacophoric features (HLM, MDR1, MLM) due to ErG's H-bond donor/acceptor encoding, and in low-data regimes (ADMET has only 560 molecules, XIMP superior in 3-4/5 tasks). For structure-dependent tasks (ESOL, FreeSolv, Lipo), conventional GNNs remain competitive. Ablation shows DIMP+MP is typically best for multi-abstraction settings (ErG+JT both active); I²MP+DIMP is most robust to abstraction choice; MP alone is least robust. Large discrepancy between validation-selected and globally best test MAE highlights hyperparameter selection challenges due to mismatch between stratified CV (target-based) and scaffold-based test splits. XIMP surpasses ECFP on most tasks, demonstrating feature learning potential. Limitations: complexity grows polynomially in n (quadratic in n for pairwise DIMP), restricted to n≤2 in practice; assumes preprocessing yields accurate graph abstraction mappings; optimal JT resolution and MP scheme combination is task-dependent. Future: extend to additional reductions, attribution tools for tracing predictions across abstractions, protein design via multi-level graph reductions.
content.dataset: MoleculeNet (ESOL, FreeSolv, Lipo), Polaris ADMET (HLM, MLM, KSOL, LogD, MDR1-MDCKII), Polaris Potency (MERS-CoV-Mpro, SARS-CoV-2-Mpro pIC50)
content.topic_relation: XIMP directly validates H8 (Message-Passing Mechanism Gap): it changes HOW information flows via cross-graph inter-message passing, not WHAT information is appended. XIMP's bipartite-style I²MP (molecular graph ↔ reduced graphs via correspondence matrices) is conceptually analogous to the PolymerBipartite candidate (atom ↔ RU virtual node communication during MP). XIMP's DIMP (direct cross-abstraction communication) creates new information pathways between abstractions — a mechanism change, not a feature addition. The compound graph formulation 𝒢(G;T₁,T₂,...,T_n) with inter-graph edges is similar to how PolymerBipartite would construct a bipartite graph connecting atoms to RU virtual nodes. XIMP also validates that interpretable abstractions as inductive bias improve low-data generalization — relevant to polymer datasets which are typically small.
content.topic_contribution: XIMP provides three actionable contributions: (1) Architecture template for PolymerBipartite — the I²MP mechanism (row-normalized correspondence matrix S_i mapping between graph levels) can be directly adapted for atom↔RU virtual node communication in polymer graphs, with RU nodes serving as the 'reduced graph' abstraction. (2) Validation that cross-level MP (not just within-level MP + late fusion) is essential — XIMP's ablation shows DIMP+MP outperforms late fusion (MP only), confirming that periodicity/fragment information must flow THROUGH message passing channels, not be appended afterward (validating HOW-vs-WHAT principle). (3) Normalization design for bipartite mapping — the ̃S_ik = D_{T,i}^{-1} S_i^⊤ D_{G,k}^{-1} S_k normalization prevents multiplicity-induced overweighting when one atom maps to multiple reduced nodes; this same issue arises in polymer graphs where one atom may belong to multiple RU boundaries. The row-stochasticity proof (Proposition 3.1/J.2) provides a theoretical foundation for stable bipartite MP in PolymerBipartite.

memory.abstract: Neural Polarization (NP) extends equivariant networks by representing each atom as a pair of an atom and a learnable virtual point whose position is updated during training, motivated by DFT polarization basis sets; NP improves prediction across QM9, MD17, xxMD, and electron density tasks, with ablations confirming that learnable VP positioning—not mere parameter increase—is the key factor.

content.background: Recent equivariant neural networks for molecular property prediction represent molecules as sets of atoms fixed in 3D space (ball-and-stick view). While this provides a concise representation of molecular configurations, it fundamentally excludes information about the surrounding atomic environments, particularly electron density configurations. DFT establishes that ground-state electron density uniquely determines all ground-state properties (Hohenberg-Kohn theorem), suggesting that models predicting quantum mechanical properties based solely on atomic positions have fundamental limitations. Prior approaches to address this gap include: (1) virtual node methods that introduce supernodes for global pattern capture (e.g., Neural Atoms, VN-EGNN), but these typically use a single or small number of nodes per molecule, not atomwise environment descriptors; (2) physics-based representations like EANN/FIREANN that encode atomic environments through density vectors; (3) direct electron density prediction models like DeepDFT. NP addresses the limitation by introducing per-atom virtual points in 3D equivariant space that can learn to represent atomwise environments including delocalized electron density, going beyond fixed-center message constraints in existing equivariant networks.
content.method: Neural Polarization (NP) is motivated by polarization basis sets in DFT, which add higher-angular-momentum functions to capture asymmetric distortions in electron density (polarization effects). The core idea: extend each atom i from a single representation (x_i, v_i) to a pair (x_i, v_i) and (x̃_i, ṽ_i), where x̃_i is a virtual point (VP) whose position is learnable and ṽ_i is its feature vector. Three-step procedure: (1) Initialization: VP positions start at atom positions (x̃₀ = x), and VP features are obtained via the same embedding layer (ṽ₀ = E(x̃₀, ã)). (2) Combined message passing: the equivariant layer M_t processes the concatenated system of 2N particles (N atoms + N VPs) using [v_{t+1}; ṽ_{t+1}] = M_t([x; x̃_t], [v_t; ṽ_t]). The same equivariant operations are applied to both atoms and VPs together, maintaining equivariance. Original atom positions x remain fixed; only VP positions x̃ are modified. (3) VP position update: a learnable projection layer π_t maps VP features to 3D position offsets: Δx̃_t = π_t(ṽ_{t+1}), then x̃_{t+1} = x̃_t + Δx̃_t (residual update). π_t is typically a simple sequential block of an equivariant layer followed by a linear layer projecting features to 3D vectors. The pooling/readout layer only uses atom features v_T (not VP features), so the output remains invariant. Key design choices: (a) VPs participate in the SAME message passing channels as atoms — they receive messages from and send messages to both atoms and other VPs, changing HOW information flows rather than WHAT is appended; (b) VP positions are LEARNABLE via π_t, not fixed — this is the critical factor per ablation studies; (c) shared weight parameters between atom and VP processing limit parameter overhead to embedding expansion and projection layers, not a full doubling; (d) NP is flexible and can be applied to most equivariant networks (EGNN, PaiNN/DeepDFT, Equiformer, TorchMD-NET) without additional regularizers or objective functions. The method is unsupervised — VPs learn their positions and features through the main task's loss function alone.
content.experiment: Four equivariant networks were selected as baselines: EGNN, DeepDFT (PaiNN-based), Equiformer, and TorchMD-NET. NP was applied to each and models were trained from scratch. Four benchmark tasks: (1) QM9 (12 targets): EGNN showed average -6.84% error reduction (9 of 12 targets improved), TorchMD-NET -5.29% (7 targets), Equiformer -4.76% (8 targets). Thermodynamic properties (U₀, U, H, G) showed -10% to -20% improvements regardless of baseline. (2) MD17 (8 molecules, TorchMD-NET baseline): average energy error -7.39%, forces -4.03% overall (-13.42% excluding naphthalene). A doubled-hidden-dimension baseline was tested: comparable or worse performance, failed to converge for benzene, severely degraded for naphthalene (energy 0.709 vs 0.085) — proving NP gains are not from parameter count. (3) xxMD (excited-state molecules, TorchMD-NET baseline): NP improved on 3 of 4 molecules (malonaldehyde, stilbene, dithiophene); azobenzene was comparable. All molecules have conjugated systems, consistent with NP capturing delocalized effects. (4) QM9 electron density (DeepDFT/PaiNN baseline): NP achieved 11.6% ε_rmse reduction and 7.0% ε_mae reduction. Critical ablation on electron density task with three variants: M1 (atom-centered VP, x̃_t = x₀): WORSE than baseline (ε_rmse 1.552% vs 0.772%) — VPs must be positioned distinctly from atoms. M2 (static offset VP, x̃_t = x*): only 3.3% ε_rmse reduction — non-learnable positioning insufficient. M3 (moving offset VP, interpolating toward x*): 5.6% reduction — layer-specific updates with non-learnable target still insufficient. NP (learnable π_t): 11.6% reduction — learnable positioning is essential. Shallow NP experiments: NP with 2 fewer layers achieved competitive or better performance than original baselines, suggesting VPs enable more efficient information propagation. Visualization of electron density predictions showed NP particularly improves in delocalized electron density regions (above/below molecular planes of conjugated systems).
content.result: NP consistently improves prediction across diverse targets and baseline architectures, with the strongest gains in thermodynamic properties (-10-20%) and electron density (11.6% ε_rmse reduction). The improvement is most pronounced for properties involving delocalized electron density (conjugated systems, thermodynamic quantities). Ablation studies conclusively demonstrate that: (1) the learnable VP position update (π_t) is the critical mechanism — static or fixed VP positions provide marginal or negative improvement; (2) performance gains are not from increased parameter count (doubled-hidden-dim baseline is worse); (3) VPs must be positioned distinctly from atom centers (M1 degrades performance). NP reduces approximation error with the original network and improves expressive power. Limitations: (1) computational cost increases due to processing 2N particles (doubled nodes and edges); (2) small molecules and complex cyclic configurations remain challenging; (3) VP trajectories (x̃) do not provide explicit knowledge about electron density despite observed directional patterns. Future directions: addressing computational complexity for large molecules, exploring other DFT-inspired extensions beyond polarization. The core principle validated: changing HOW information flows during message passing (via learnable virtual points participating in the same channels as atoms) is more effective than adding information (WHAT) afterward.

memory.content:
Day 5 Experiment: PolymerBipartite v2 — FAILED (Negative Result)

## Idea Tested
H8 (Message-Passing Mechanism Gap): The 50→30 RMSE gap requires changing HOW periodicity flows during message passing, not WHAT information is appended. PolymerBipartite v2 injects periodicity at the NODE level via RU virtual nodes with XIMP-style iterative atom↔RU inter-message passing, gated RU→atom broadcast, and inter-RU coupling.

## Hypothesis
If mechanism change is correct, PolymerBipartite v2 should achieve RMSE <50 (breaking the 50-54 ceiling) because periodicity flows through the same MP channels as atomic features via RU virtual nodes, with gated communication preventing VN flooding.

## Experimental Results

### Iteration 1 (MLP gates, warmup discriminability)
- BPv2 multi-seed: 55.22 ± 1.04 (WORSE than baseline 53.41 ± 0.93)
- Gate collapse: all gates ≈ 1.0 (flat broadcast = VN flooding)
- RU cos_sim: 71.8% pairs > 0.95 (near-degenerate)
- Random RU delta: +3.04 (real assignment better, but overall performance worse)
- Parameter-matched baseline: RMSE=124 (broken — added 73 extra layers)

### Iteration 2 (scalar gates, stronger discriminability, gradient clipping, separate LR, LayerNorm)
- BPv2 multi-seed: 53.81 ± 0.94 (within noise of baseline 54.00 ± 1.96)
- Gate fix worked: boundary=0.285, interior=0.062 (4.6x ratio, differentiated)
- RU cos_sim: 30.4% pairs > 0.95 (improved but still partially degenerate)
- Random RU delta: +0.03 (NEGLIGIBLE — real assignment provides virtually no information)
- Wide parameter-matched baseline: 53.66 (BEATS BPv2 53.81)

## Critical Negative Findings

1. **Random RU assignment matches real assignment (delta=+0.03)**: This is the most damning evidence. The bipartite structure (which atoms belong to which RU, which are boundary vs interior) provides NO useful periodicity information for Tg prediction. The RU virtual nodes are not extracting meaningful inter-RU coupling signals.

2. **Wide parameter-matched baseline beats BPv2**: The extra 1M parameters allocated to the RU channel would be better used by simply widening a standard GIN (h=408 → 53.66 vs BPv2 53.81). The bipartite mechanism is not extracting information that wider standard MP can't already capture.

3. **RU representations partially collapse**: Despite stronger discriminability regularizer (λ=0.1, margin=0.85, no warmup), 30.4% of RU pairs still have cos_sim > 0.95. RU representations trend toward similarity during training, suggesting the RU channel doesn't learn discriminative periodicity features.

4. **Gate fix worked but didn't improve performance**: The scalar gate fix (boundary=0.285, interior=0.062) successfully differentiated boundary and interior atoms, but this didn't translate to better Tg prediction. The RU channel's content is not useful regardless of how it's routed.

5. **Training instability persists**: Val RMSE oscillated in both iterations, suggesting the RU channel introduces noise that destabilizes learning.

## Why It Failed — Root Cause Analysis

The fundamental issue is that on a TRIMER graph (3 repeat units, 30-60 atoms), standard GIN message passing with 5 layers already reaches across RU boundaries. Every atom can receive messages from atoms in adjacent RUs through the existing bond structure. The RU virtual nodes are therefore REDUNDANT with the atom-level message passing — they aggregate information that atoms already have access to.

This is analogous to the BlochSpec failure (graph-level features redundant with MP) and the Small-Graph Paradox (Transformer attention redundant on small graphs). The RU virtual nodes are a third instance of the same principle: on sufficiently small graphs, any additional communication channel that aggregates information already reachable through existing MP is redundant.

The "Message-Passing Mechanism Gap" (H8) may still exist, but it cannot be bridged by adding redundant communication channels on top of existing MP. The gap requires either:
(a) A fundamentally different MP mechanism (not additive — e.g., Chemprop's directed bond-level messages which process information differently, not just add another channel)
(b) A different graph representation where the RU structure provides genuinely NEW information not already reachable (e.g., periodic edges in PerioGT's representation)
(c) Pre-training at a scale where the RU structure provides genuinely NEW priors (not just regularization)

## Impact on Hypothesis Space

H8 (Message-Passing Mechanism Gap) is NOT supported by PolymerBipartite v2 evidence. The bipartite atom↔RU mechanism does not extract useful periodicity information beyond what standard GIN already captures through its 5-layer MP on trimer graphs.

However, H8 is not completely invalidated — the mechanism gap may still exist, but it requires a QUALITATIVELY different mechanism (not just adding a redundant channel). The three remaining candidates:
- Chemprop-Polymer: directed bond-level messages on periodic edges (qualitatively different MP mechanism)
- Equivariant MP: periodicity-conditioned attention (different computational paradigm)
- Or: the 50→30 gap may require pre-training at PI1M scale with architecture-SSL co-design that genuinely changes the representation space

## MetaMethod Lessons

1. **Redundant Channel Principle**: On small graphs where MP already reaches all nodes, adding another communication channel (RU virtual nodes) that aggregates information already reachable through existing MP is redundant. This is a generalization of both the Small-Graph Paradox and the Feature Injection Redundancy Principle.

2. **Random Assignment Control is Essential**: The random RU assignment control (delta=+0.03) was the most informative diagnostic. It revealed that the bipartite structure provides NO useful periodicity information, which would have been impossible to discover from performance alone.

3. **Gate Fix ≠ Performance Fix**: Fixing a technical bug (gate collapse) improved the mechanism's functioning but didn't improve performance. The underlying issue was not how the gate worked, but whether the RU channel carried useful information at all.

4. **Parameter Matching Must Use Width, Not Depth**: Adding 73 extra linear layers (iter1) broke the model completely (RMSE=124). Widening hidden dim (iter2, h=408) was a fair comparison that revealed the baseline actually benefits more from extra parameters than BPv2.

Day 5 Journal — Polymer Deep Learning Research

**Learning**: Read XIMP (bipartite atom↔fragment MP for non-local interactions), Virtual Points (learnable VN features updated during MP), HSG (small graph insights: single-level VNs, top-layer pooling). Key design insights: iterative inter-message passing (not one-shot), gated/attention-weighted messages (essential), learnable VN features (not fixed).

**Experiments**: PolymerBipartite v2 — TWO iterations, both FAILED.
- Iteration 1 (MLP gates, warmup discriminability): Multi-seed 55.22±1.04 (WORSE than baseline 53.41±0.93). Gate collapse (all ≈1.0). RU cos_sim 71.8% >0.95.
- Iteration 2 (scalar gates, stronger discriminability, gradient clipping, separate LR, LayerNorm): Multi-seed 53.81±0.94 (within noise of baseline 54.00±1.96). Gate fix worked (boundary=0.285, interior=0.062). But random RU delta=+0.03 (NEGLIGIBLE). Wide parameter-matched baseline beats BPv2 (53.66 vs 53.81).

**Root Cause**: On trimer graphs (30-60 atoms, 5 GIN layers), standard MP already reaches across RU boundaries. RU virtual nodes aggregate information that atoms already have access to — they are REDUNDANT with existing MP. This is the Redundant Channel Principle: on small graphs where MP already reaches all nodes, adding another communication channel is redundant.

**Internalization**: FOUR paradigms now EXHAUSTED:
1. Contrastive pre-training (variance reduction only, not mean improvement)
2. GIN architecture innovation (GAT, VN, GPS all increase overfitting)
3. Graph-level feature injection (redundant with MP)
4. Bipartite MP channels (redundant with existing MP on small graphs)

The 50→30 gap requires a QUALITATIVELY different approach:
- Chemprop-Polymer: directed bond-level messages on periodic edges (different computational paradigm, not just additive channel)
- Or: fundamentally different representation where periodicity provides genuinely NEW information (periodic edges, not just larger graphs)
- Or: the gap may require pre-training at PI1M scale with architecture that genuinely uses periodicity priors

**Ideas for Day 6**: Chemprop-Polymer v2 (directed bond messages on periodic edges — qualitatively different MP mechanism), Periodic Edge GIN (add periodic edges to trimer graph as in Antoniuk et al.), or reconsider whether the 50→30 gap is achievable with current dataset size and architecture constraints.

H2 (Architecture-SSL Co-Design): EXHAUSTED — simple MPNN + PA contrastive pre-training alone is insufficient.

H6 (Monomer Encoder Degeneracy): VALIDATED — monomer-level GIN encoders produce near-degenerate representations (cos_sim=0.963).
H7 (Feature Injection Redundancy): VALIDATED — graph-level features redundant with MP.

H8 (Message-Passing Mechanism Change): PARTIALLY INVALIDATED — PolymerBipartite v2 (bipartite atom↔RU MP) FAILED. The mechanism change must be QUALITATIVELY different (different computational paradigm), not just adding another channel. Adding redundant channels on small graphs doesn't help.

H9 (Redundant Channel Principle — NEW): On small graphs where MP already reaches all nodes (trimer with 30-60 atoms, 5 GIN layers), any additional communication channel that aggregates information already reachable through existing MP is redundant. This generalizes the Small-Graph Paradox (Transformer attention redundant) and Feature Injection Redundancy (graph-level features redundant) to a third case: bipartite MP channels redundant. The principle predicts that ANY additive mechanism on top of existing MP will fail on these graphs — the gap requires changing the MP mechanism itself (not adding to it).

H10 (Qualitative Mechanism Change — NEW): The 50→30 gap requires changing the MP mechanism in a way that provides genuinely NEW computational paths, not just additional channels. Chemprop's directed bond-level messages process information along a different computational axis (bond direction) that may capture periodicity in a way atom-level undirected MP cannot. Periodic edges add genuinely NEW connectivity that doesn't exist in the trimer graph. Both change the fundamental computational graph, not just add channels to it.
