Solution: (1) freeze Chemprop encoder after standard or multi-task training, (2) replace FFN with kernel ridge regression on embeddings, (3) augment embeddings with kernel mean embedding of node-level distributions to preserve distributional information that global pooling destroys, (4) optionally condition encoder with multi-task auxiliary losses from MD-computed polymer properties (density, refractive index, Cp) to force physics-relevant embedding structure
memory.keyword: prediction-head bottleneck, kernel ridge regression, decoupled encoder, kernel mean embedding, multi-task conditioning

H: H13a (Prediction-Head Bottleneck): The 43→30 gap is fundamentally a prediction-head bottleneck, not an encoder bottleneck. Chemprop's underfitting signal (negative overfitting gaps across ALL ablations, mem_144) indicates the encoder has MORE capacity than the training data can fill — the encoder is producing embeddings that contain more information than the 2-layer FFN can extract. The FFN (2 hidden layers, 300 neurons each, ~180K parameters) maps a 300-dim continuous embedding to a single Tg value through a smooth, relatively simple nonlinear function. But Tg is NOT a smooth function of chemical structure — it depends on discrete structural features (presence/absence of aromatic rings, polar groups, specific backbone types) that create sharp transitions in the Tg landscape. A polymer with an aromatic backbone has Tg ~400K; replacing one aromatic ring with an alkyl chain drops Tg by ~100K. This is a PIECEWISE, DISCONTINUOUS mapping that a 2-layer FFN struggles to learn because ReLU networks produce smooth interpolations between training points. The encoder may already encode these discrete features in its 300-dim embedding space, but the FFN cannot extract the sharp, piecewise mapping needed to convert them to accurate Tg predictions. Evidence: (a) negative overfitting gaps = encoder has unused capacity, (b) Chemprop achieves 43.46 with a simple FFN — what if a better predictor on the SAME embeddings achieves 30? (c) In NLP, linear probes on frozen pre-trained representations often match or exceed end-to-end fine-tuning (Kumar et al. 2022), suggesting the representation already contains the answer and the prediction mechanism is the bottleneck.

H13b (Decoupled Optimization Enables Better Representations): End-to-end training entangles the encoder and predictor — the encoder learns to produce embeddings that the SIMPLE FFN can easily map to Tg, not embeddings that are MAXIMALLY INFORMATIVE about Tg. This is a representation-predictor alignment problem: the encoder optimizes for the predictor's limitations, not for maximal information content. Decoupling breaks this entanglement: (a) the encoder can be trained independently (with multi-task auxiliary losses on diverse polymer properties) to produce maximally informative, physics-relevant embeddings, and (b) the kernel predictor (KRR/GPR) can then learn the optimal nonlinear mapping from these embeddings to Tg without being constrained by the FFN's limited expressiveness. KRR with RBF kernel can learn ANY continuous nonlinear mapping (universal approximation in RKHS), including sharp piecewise transitions, because the kernel function implicitly projects into an infinite-dimensional feature space where such mappings become linear. On 7170 samples, KRR is well within its comfort zone — kernel methods are known to outperform neural networks on datasets of this size (mem_063, mem_033).

H13c (Kernel Mean Embedding Preserves Distributional Information Lost by Pooling): Chemprop uses global_mean_pool to collapse all node embeddings into a single 300-dim vector. This destroys critical distributional information: two polymers with very different internal structures (e.g., one with a rigid aromatic backbone and flexible side chains, another with a uniform semi-rigid structure) can produce the same mean embedding if their node embeddings average to the same vector. Tg depends on the DISTRIBUTION of structural features across the polymer — specifically, whether certain critical features (backbone rigidity, polar groups) are present in specific regions. The kernel mean embedding (KME, mem_063) of the node-level embedding distribution preserves this information: instead of computing mean_pool(h_nodes), compute φ_KME = [Σ_i w_i · k(g_j, h_node_i)] for j=1,...,d grid points, where k is an RBF kernel and g_j are grid points spanning the embedding space. This d-dimensional vector captures the FULL distributional shape of node embeddings — including multimodality (some nodes in aromatic regions, others in flexible regions) that mean pooling collapses. Concatenating the KME descriptor with the mean-pooled embedding gives the kernel predictor access to both the overall embedding (what the polymer 'looks like on average') and the distributional structure (how structural features are distributed across the polymer). This is NOT redundant with mean pooling because KME captures information that pooling explicitly destroys — analogous to how variance captures information that the mean alone cannot.
X:
DEKP Architecture and Implementation:

Phase 1: Encoder Training (standard or multi-task)

Option A (Simple): Train Chemprop-Polymer exactly as Day 5 (depth=3, hidden_dim=300, polymer graph with periodic edge, standard 2-layer FFN prediction head, MSE loss on Tg). After training converges, REMOVE the FFN prediction head and FREEZE the encoder. This is the simplest version — the encoder is trained purely for Tg, and we test whether a kernel predictor on the same embeddings outperforms the FFN.

Option B (Multi-task conditioned): Train Chemprop-Polymer with auxiliary property losses alongside Tg. Auxiliary properties sourced from:
(a) RadonPy MD-computed properties (mem_057): density, refractive index, Cp, expansion coefficients — available for ~1000 polymers
(b) Literature datasets: melting temperature Tm (~942 polymers from mem_033), density (~382 polymers), modulus (~306 polymers)
(c) Computed descriptors: rotatable bond fraction, aromatic content, molecular weight — available for ALL 7170 polymers via RDKit

Multi-task architecture: Shared Chemprop encoder → separate prediction heads for each property. Total loss: L = L_Tg + Σ_k α_k · L_aux_k. Auxiliary losses force the encoder to learn features relevant to MULTIPLE physical properties, not just Tg. This produces embeddings with richer physics content.

Key: auxiliary data is SPARSE (different properties have different coverage). Use masked multi-task training: for each polymer, compute loss only on properties with available labels. This is exactly polyGNN's approach (mem_071) with selector vectors.

CRITICAL: After multi-task training, REMOVE all prediction heads and FREEZE the encoder. The encoder now produces embeddings conditioned on multiple physics-relevant properties.

Phase 2: Embedding Extraction

For ALL 7170 polymers in the Tg dataset:
1. Forward-pass each polymer's trimer graph through the frozen Chemprop encoder
2. Extract TWO types of embeddings:
   (a) Graph-level embedding: h_graph = mean_pool(h_nodes) ∈ R^300 (standard Chemprop output)
   (b) Node-level KME descriptor: φ_KME ∈ R^(d×K) where:
      - K = number of component features extracted per node (e.g., 5: atomic number, degree, electronegativity, aromaticity, partial charge)
      - d = number of grid points per feature (d=10 initially, tunable)
      - For each component feature λ_k and grid point g_j:
        φ_KME[k,j] = Σ_i (1/N) · exp(-||g_j - λ_k(h_node_i)||² / (2σ_k²))
      - σ_k = median heuristic (set to median pairwise distance of λ_k values across all nodes in all polymers)
      - Total KME dimension: d×K = 10×5 = 50 (compact, not overwhelming)
   (c) Combined embedding: h_combined = h_graph ⊕ φ_KME ∈ R^350 (300 + 50)
3. Store embeddings as numpy arrays for fast KRR training

Compute time: ~5 minutes for 7170 polymers (single forward pass per polymer, no gradients)

Phase 3: Kernel Ridge Regression on Embeddings

Train KRR with RBF kernel on the combined embeddings:

k(h_i, h_j) = exp(-||h_i - h_j||² / (2σ²))

where σ is the kernel bandwidth (optimized via grid search on validation set).

KRR solution: α = (K + λI)^(-1) · y
where K is the 5164×5164 kernel matrix (training set), λ is regularization, y is Tg values.

Prediction: Tg_pred = Σ_i α_i · k(h_test, h_i)

Hyperparameter optimization:
- σ: grid search over {0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0} × median pairwise distance
- λ: grid search over {1e-6, 1e-4, 1e-2, 1e0, 1e2}
- Use 5-fold cross-validation on training set for selection, then evaluate on test set

Alternative: Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) with RBF kernel — provides uncertainty estimates and automatic hyperparameter optimization via marginal likelihood maximization. Same predictive performance as KRR but with uncertainty.

Alternative: KRR with composite kernel:
k_composite(h_i, h_j) = k_RBF(h_graph_i, h_graph_j) + k_RBF(φ_KME_i, φ_KME_j)
This allows different bandwidths for the graph-level and distributional-level components, recognizing that they live in different scales.

Phase 4: Multi-Seed Verification and Diagnostics

All experiments with ≥3 seeds (seeds {42, 71, 123}).

Mandatory diagnostics:
1. Overfitting gap comparison: KRR overfitting gap vs FFN overfitting gap. Expected: KRR gap < FFN gap (kernel methods are inherently well-regularized).
2. Embedding information content: Train a LINEAR regression on h_graph alone (no kernel, no KME). If linear RMSE ≈ 43-45: the embedding contains Tg-relevant information in a linearly accessible form. If linear RMSE ≈ 55-60: the information is nonlinearly encoded, requiring a kernel to extract.
3. KME incremental value: Compare KRR on h_graph alone vs KRR on h_combined (h_graph + φ_KME). If KME adds >2 RMSE improvement: distributional information matters. If KME adds <1 RMSE: mean pooling already captures sufficient information.
4. Random KME control: Replace φ_KME with random vectors of same dimension and distribution statistics. If random matches real: KME provides dimensionality, not physics information. If real outperforms random: KME captures genuine distributional structure.
5. Encoder-predictor decoupling diagnostic: Compare (a) end-to-end Chemprop with FFN (43.46 baseline) vs (b) frozen Chemprop encoder + KRR on same embeddings. If (b) > (a): the FFN was the bottleneck. If (b) ≈ (a): the encoder is the bottleneck (KRR can't improve on what the FFN already extracts).
6. Multi-task conditioning diagnostic: Compare KRR on simple-encoder embeddings vs KRR on multi-task-encoder embeddings. If multi-task > simple by >3 RMSE: auxiliary losses improve embedding quality. If multi-task ≈ simple: Tg-specific training already produces optimal embeddings.
7. Kernel bandwidth analysis: Plot test RMSE vs kernel bandwidth σ. Should show a clear optimum. If optimum is at very small σ: the mapping is highly nonlinear (sharp transitions). If optimum is at large σ: the mapping is nearly linear (FFN could learn it).

Key Ablations (all with multi-seed ≥3 seeds):

(a) Chemprop+FFN end-to-end (Day 5 baseline = 43.46±0.89) — reference
(b) Frozen Chemprop encoder (Tg-only training) + KRR on h_graph — tests H13a: prediction-head bottleneck
(c) Frozen Chemprop encoder (Tg-only training) + KRR on h_combined (h_graph + φ_KME) — tests H13a+H13c
(d) Frozen Chemprop encoder (Tg-only training) + LINEAR regression on h_graph — baseline for linear accessibility
(e) Frozen Chemprop encoder (Tg-only training) + GPR on h_combined — uncertainty-aware variant
(f) Frozen Chemprop encoder (Tg-only training) + KRR on h_graph + φ_KME_RANDOM — random KME control
(g) Frozen Chemprop encoder (multi-task training with density, refractive index, Cp, rotatable bond fraction) + KRR on h_combined — tests H13a+H13b+H13c (FULL MODEL)
(h) Frozen Chemprop encoder (multi-task training) + KRR on h_graph alone — tests H13b without H13c
(i) Frozen Chemprop encoder (multi-task training) + FFN (standard 2-layer prediction head) — tests whether multi-task helps even with FFN
(j) KRR on φ_KME alone (no h_graph) — tests whether distributional information alone is sufficient
(k) KRR on RDKit descriptors only (no Chemprop embeddings) — pure descriptor baseline, ~45-50 RMSE expected
(l) KRR on h_graph + RDKit descriptors — tests whether chemical descriptors complement embeddings
(m) Chemprop+FFN with deeper prediction head (4 hidden layers instead of 2) — tests whether FFN capacity is the bottleneck (if deeper FFN matches KRR, the issue was FFN depth, not FFN vs kernel)
(n) KRR on Chemprop embeddings from DEEPER encoder (depth=5) — tests whether encoder depth + kernel predictor are complementary
Y: If H13a correct: Frozen Chemprop encoder + KRR (ablation b) should significantly outperform end-to-end Chemprop+FFN (ablation a, 43.46). Expected: KRR → ~35-40 RMSE (3-8 improvement). The kernel predictor extracts nonlinear mapping that the FFN cannot. The improvement comes purely from changing the PREDICTION MECHANISM, not the encoder. This would be a paradigm-shifting result: the 43→30 gap is a prediction-head problem, not an encoder problem.

If H13a partially correct: KRR improves by 2-4 RMSE over FFN (expected ~39-41). The prediction head is a partial bottleneck — some of the gap is prediction-head, some is encoder. Combining with multi-task conditioning (H13b) and KME (H13c) may close more of the gap.

If H13a incorrect: KRR matches or worsens FFN performance (~43-45). The FFN already extracts the optimal mapping from the embeddings. The 43→30 gap is entirely an encoder problem — the embeddings don't contain enough information for 30 RMSE regardless of the predictor. This would validate the current paradigm (encoder improvement is the only path).

If H13b correct: Multi-task-conditioned encoder + KRR (ablation g) should outperform Tg-only encoder + KRR (ablation c). Expected delta: ~3-5 RMSE points. Auxiliary losses force the encoder to learn physics-relevant features (backbone rigidity, polar interactions, aromatic content) that are relevant to Tg but may not be optimally encoded when training only on Tg. The multi-task encoder produces embeddings where Tg-relevant information is more explicitly represented, making it easier for the kernel predictor to extract.

If H13b incorrect: Multi-task conditioning doesn't improve KRR performance. The Tg-only encoder already produces optimal embeddings for Tg prediction. Auxiliary losses add noise or distort the embedding space away from Tg-relevant features. This would mean the encoder doesn't need multi-task conditioning — the bottleneck is purely the prediction mechanism.

If H13c correct: KRR on h_combined (h_graph + φ_KME) (ablation c) should outperform KRR on h_graph alone (ablation b). Expected delta: ~2-4 RMSE points. The distributional information captured by KME provides genuinely new information about how structural features are distributed across the polymer — information that mean pooling destroys. Random KME control (ablation f) should perform worse than real KME, confirming that the specific distributional structure matters.

If H13c incorrect: KME adds <1 RMSE improvement. Mean pooling already captures sufficient information for Tg prediction. The distributional structure of node embeddings is redundant with the mean. Random KME matches real KME. This would mean the graph-level embedding is sufficient — the distributional information is not needed.

Expected best result: ~32-37 RMSE with multi-task-conditioned encoder + KRR on h_combined. This closes most of the 43→30 gap through a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT MECHANISM (prediction-head replacement + multi-task conditioning + distributional preservation) rather than encoder improvement. If this achieves ~30.8 or better: the prediction-head bottleneck hypothesis is validated — the 43→30 gap was never about the encoder.

If the full model achieves ~35-38: significant improvement (5-8 over baseline), validating H13a partially. The remaining gap may require: (a) better auxiliary property data (more polymers with MD-computed properties), (b) richer KME descriptors (more component features, more grid points), or (c) hybrid approach combining encoder improvement with kernel predictor.

Diagnostic: Linear regression on h_graph (ablation d). If linear RMSE ≈ 50-55: Tg is a highly nonlinear function of the embedding, and the kernel is essential for extracting it. If linear RMSE ≈ 40-43: Tg is approximately linear in the embedding, and the FFN's nonlinear layers add minimal value — the gap is about regularization, not expressiveness. If linear RMSE ≈ 43-45: the FFN is already near-optimal for the linear component, and the kernel helps with the residual nonlinear component.

Diagnostic: Kernel bandwidth optimum. If the optimal σ is small (σ < 0.5 × median distance): the Tg-embedding mapping has sharp transitions (piecewise behavior), confirming that Tg depends on discrete structural features. This validates the prediction-head bottleneck — the FFN cannot learn sharp transitions. If σ is large (σ > 2 × median distance): the mapping is smooth, and the FFN should be able to learn it — the prediction-head bottleneck hypothesis is weakened.

Diagnostic: Deeper FFN (ablation m). If 4-layer FFN matches KRR performance: the issue was FFN depth/capacity, not FFN vs kernel fundamentally. The kernel is just a more efficient way to add prediction capacity. If 4-layer FFN still underperforms KRR by >3 RMSE: the kernel provides genuinely different prediction capability (infinite-dimensional RKHS projection) that deeper FFNs cannot replicate — a stronger validation of H13a.

Diagnostic: Multi-task + FFN (ablation i). If multi-task conditioning improves FFN performance by ~2-3 RMSE but KRR on the same embeddings improves by ~5-8 RMSE: multi-task helps the encoder, but the prediction mechanism is still the bottleneck. The total improvement from multi-task + KRR should be SUPERADDITIVE if both H13a and H13b are correct.

Progressive strategy: If DEKP achieves ~32-37, the remaining gap to 30.8 may be closed by: (a) adding conformer landscape features (CEL, mem_137) as additional KRR inputs, (b) using a composite kernel that combines RBF on embeddings + RBF on physics-computed features, (c) scaling multi-task auxiliary data with more MD-computed properties from RadonPy for more polymers.

memory.abstract: KPGT proposes a self-supervised learning framework for molecular property prediction that addresses two key issues—ill-defined pre-training tasks and limited model capacity—by introducing a Line Graph Transformer (LiGhT) that elevates chemical bonds to nodes via line graph transformation, and a knowledge-guided pre-training strategy that uses molecular descriptors and fingerprints as semantic guidance for masked node prediction, achieving state-of-the-art results on 11 downstream datasets.

content.background: Molecular property prediction is critical for drug and material discovery, but supervised deep learning models suffer from poor performance due to limited labeled data and the vast chemical space. Self-supervised learning (SSL) on molecular graphs has emerged as a promising direction, leveraging large-scale unlabeled molecules for pre-training. However, the authors identify two major issues hindering current SSL methods: (1) Ill-defined pre-training tasks — generative methods (masking nodes/edges/subgraphs) lose molecular semantics because even small modifications to molecular graphs can drastically change properties (unlike word masking in NLP or image augmentation in CV, which preserve fundamental semantics). The dependence between masked nodes and neighbors is weak (only valency rules), causing the model to potentially memorize rather than learn. Contrastive methods suffer similarly because graph augmentations (node dropping, edge perturbation) alter fundamental molecular characteristics. (2) Limited model capacity — most SSL methods use GIN as backbone, which provides limited capacity insufficient for capturing the wide range of information needed for diverse molecular properties. Transformer-based architectures, proven highly effective in NLP and CV, remain underexplored for molecular graph SSL. These two issues together explain why current SSL methods capture only structural similarity and simple construction rules, failing to induce abundant semantics related to molecular properties.
content.method:
KPGT consists of two core components: Line Graph Transformer (LiGhT) and a knowledge-guided pre-training strategy.

**LiGhT (Line Graph Transformer)**:
The key insight is that chemical bonds carry rich information (bond type, stereo, conjugation, ring membership) that previous graph transformers either omit or only use as attention bias. LiGhT elevates bonds to first-class citizens via line graph transformation:
- Line graph construction: Each edge e_{i,j} in the original molecular graph becomes a node v_{i,j} in the line graph. Two edges sharing a common atom in the original graph become connected nodes in the line graph.
- Node feature initialization: h_{v_{i,j}} = concat(W_v*x_i^v + W_v*x_j^v, W_e*x_{i,j}^e), combining both endpoint atom features (summed and projected) and bond features (projected). This gives bonds full representational power rather than being secondary edge attributes.
- Architecture: Classic transformer encoder (12 layers, 768 hidden dim, 12 attention heads, ~100M parameters) with two structural encoding mechanisms injected into the self-attention:
  - **Path Encoding**: For each pair of nodes in the line graph, compute the shortest path, then average the projected features of all nodes along the path and project to an attention scalar a_{i,j}^p. Unlike previous methods that only encode edge features along paths, LiGhT encodes complete path node features.
  - **Distance Encoding**: Encode the shortest path distance between node pairs through a 2-layer MLP (GELU activation) to produce attention scalar a_{i,j}^d.
  - Modified attention: A^{l,k} = softmax(QK^T/sqrt(D_h) + A^p + A^d). Both encodings are added as bias to the attention matrix, preserving structural inductive bias while maintaining the global receptive field of transformers.
- Mean pooling over all nodes produces the molecular representation.

**Knowledge-Guided Pre-training Strategy**:
The core problem with standard generative pre-training (masked node prediction) is that masking loses semantics and the dependence between masked nodes and neighbors is weak (valency rules alone cannot uniquely determine the masked atom). KPGT addresses this by introducing molecular knowledge as semantic guidance:
- **Knowledge Node (K node)**: A special virtual node connected to every node in the line graph. Its raw features are initialized with 200 molecular descriptors (quantitative physicochemical profiles, e.g., LogP) and 512 RDKit fingerprints (bit strings indicating substructure existence), all readily available from RDKit at no extra cost.
- **Masking scheme**: Randomly mask 50% of line graph nodes (80% replaced with mask token, 10% random node, 10% unchanged) AND mask 50% of K node features simultaneously.
- **Pre-training objectives**: (1) Predict original node types of masked nodes (cross-entropy loss) — the K node's remaining (unmasked) knowledge guides this prediction by providing semantic context. (2) Predict masked molecular descriptors (RMSE regression loss). (3) Predict masked fingerprints (binary cross-entropy classification loss).
- **Mechanism**: The K node participates in self-attention, so unmasked knowledge features flow through attention to guide masked node prediction. This replaces the weak valency-rule dependence with rich semantic dependence. The knowledge serves as the semantics lost in the masked graph.
- The 50% masking rate (much higher than typical 15%) is optimal because the knowledge guidance makes aggressive masking feasible — the model must rely on semantic information rather than memorization.
content.experiment:
**Pre-training**: 2 million unique unlabeled molecular SMILES from ChEMBL29 dataset. Molecular graphs constructed via RDKit. 12-layer LiGhT, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads, ~100M parameters. Adam optimizer (lr=2e-4, weight decay=1e-6), batch size 1024, 100K steps, masking rate 0.5 for both nodes and knowledge. Pre-training took ~2 days on 4 Nvidia A100 GPUs.

**Downstream evaluation**: 11 datasets — 8 classification (BACE, BBBP, ClinTox, SIDER, Estrogen, MetStab, Tox21, ToxCast) and 3 regression (FreeSolv, ESOL, Lipophilicity). Scaffold splitting (8:1:1), 3 random seeds, report mean±std. Two settings: feature extraction (frozen backbone + trained predictor) and transfer learning (fine-tune all parameters). Predictor: 2-layer MLP with ReLU. 48 hyper-parameter combinations grid-searched per task.

**Baselines**: 12 SSL methods — 6 generative (Edgepred, Masking, Contextpred, Masking+Sup, Contextpred+Sup, GROVER) and 6 contrastive (Infomax, GraphLoG, GraphCL, JOAO, 3DInfomax, GraphMVP).

**Ablation studies**:
1. Backbone comparison: LiGhT vs GIN, vanilla Transformer, Graphormer (all ~3.5M params, same pre-training strategy). LiGhT consistently best (classification AVG 0.829 vs 0.817/0.822/0.826; regression AVG 1.162 vs 1.229/1.260/1.189).
2. Pre-training effectiveness: KPGT (pre-trained LiGhT) vs LiGhT (no pre-training). Relative improvement: 5.1% classification, 18.8% regression.
3. Knowledge vs direct feature use: KPGT outperforms MD+FP (direct descriptor+fingerprint concatenation through MLP) and GROVER+FP (GROVER representations + fingerprints), confirming that the knowledge-guided pre-training learns semantics beyond the introduced knowledge itself.
4. Masking rate: 15%→0.827/1.228, 30%→0.835/1.216, 50%→0.843/1.175 (best), 60%→0.832/1.186. Optimal 50% is much higher than typical 15%, indicating knowledge guidance enables aggressive masking.
content.result:
KPGT achieves state-of-the-art performance across all 11 datasets under both evaluation settings. Feature extraction setting: overall 5% relative improvement (3.5% classification, 8.9% regression). Transfer learning setting: overall 3.9% improvement (2.2% classification, 8.3% regression). Key findings:

1. Knowledge incorporation is crucial: Methods with additional knowledge (Contextpred+Sup, Masking+Sup, GROVER) generally outperform those without, validating that molecular semantics are essential for effective pre-training.

2. High-capacity backbone matters: GROVER (transformer, ~100M params) outperforms GIN-based methods, confirming that model capacity is a key factor.

3. KPGT's knowledge-guided strategy learns beyond the introduced knowledge: It outperforms simply concatenating the same descriptors/fingerprints as input features, indicating the pre-training process internalizes semantic information into the representation rather than just providing an additional feature channel.

4. Catastrophic forgetting concern: On some datasets (BACE, SIDER, MetStab), transfer learning shows comparable or worse results than feature extraction, suggesting fine-tuning strategies need further exploration.

5. The 50% optimal masking rate (vs 15% in BERT-style methods) demonstrates that when proper semantic guidance exists, aggressive masking forces meaningful learning rather than memorization.

**Limitations**: The additional knowledge (descriptors/fingerprints) is derived from 2D molecular structure via RDKit, so it does not capture 3D geometric information. The line graph transformation increases graph size (edges become nodes), potentially increasing computational cost for large molecules. Fine-tuning can suffer from catastrophic forgetting on some tasks. Future directions include incorporating 3D geometry, exploring better fine-tuning strategies, and collecting more carefully curated molecular knowledge.

content.topic_relation:
KPGT directly relates to multiple active hypotheses in our TopicState:
- H4/H8a (Message-Passing Mechanism Gap / Architecture Mechanism Dominance): KPGT's line graph transformation elevates bonds to nodes, making bond information the primary representational unit. This validates our finding that bond-level mechanisms dominate atom-level mechanisms (14:1 ratio). The line graph approach is a different implementation of the same principle — bonds carry the most important information.
- H10 (Redundant Channel Principle): KPGT's K node (knowledge node) is an additional channel, but it brings genuinely external knowledge (descriptors/fingerprints computed from RDKit, not re-encoding reachable graph structure). This is exactly boundary condition (b) of H10 — pre-trained channels bringing genuinely external knowledge are NOT redundant. The fact that KPGT outperforms MD+FP (direct feature concatenation) confirms that the knowledge-guided pre-training internalizes semantics into representations rather than just adding a redundant feature channel.
- H11 (Paradigm Re-evaluation on Chemprop): KPGT demonstrates that knowledge-guided pre-training on a high-capacity transformer backbone works synergistically. This supports our plan to re-evaluate contrastive pre-training on Chemprop — the key is that pre-training must bring external knowledge, not just re-encode reachable structure.
- The 50% optimal masking rate vs 15% is relevant to our pre-training design — when semantic guidance is available, aggressive masking is beneficial.
content.topic_contribution:
KPGT provides several actionable insights for our polymer deep learning research:
1. **Knowledge-guided pre-training for Chemprop**: Instead of pure contrastive pre-training on PI1M, consider a knowledge-guided approach where polymer-specific descriptors (e.g., Tg-related features, chain flexibility indices, monomer complexity metrics) serve as semantic guidance during pre-training. This aligns with H11's priority of bringing genuinely external knowledge through pre-training.
2. **Bond-centric representation validates our architecture choice**: KPGT's success with line graphs (bonds as nodes) reinforces our Chemprop-Polymer direction — bond-level directed message passing is the right mechanism. We should NOT revert to atom-level architectures.
3. **Higher masking rates with knowledge guidance**: When implementing pre-training for Chemprop on PI1M, consider masking rates of 30-50% rather than 15%, especially if we incorporate polymer knowledge (computed descriptors) as guidance.
4. **Knowledge injection via virtual node**: The K node design (virtual node connected to all nodes, initialized with external knowledge) is a concrete architectural pattern we could adapt for Chemprop — add a polymer-knowledge virtual node during pre-training that carries computed polymer descriptors.
5. **Pre-training internalizes beyond raw features**: KPGT outperforming MD+FP confirms that the pre-training process itself creates better representations than simply adding features as input. This means our Chemprop + PI1M pre-training should focus on the pre-training process design, not just feature engineering.

memory.abstract: DenseGNN combines Dense Connectivity Network (DCN), hierarchical node-edge-graph residual networks (HRN), and Local Structure Order Parameters Embedding (LOPE) to create a universal, scalable GNN that overcomes over-smoothing (supporting 60+ GC layers), reduces edge connectivity costs via LOPE, and achieves SOTA on Matbench, JARVIS-DFT, QM9, and OC22 datasets across crystal, molecular, and catalysis domains.

content.background: GNNs have become a dominant approach for predicting material properties due to their ability to directly operate on graph representations of molecules and crystals. However, three key problems persist in practical applications: (1) Nested graph network strategies (e.g., ALIGNN, coNGN) that incorporate bond angle information substantially increase trainable parameters and training costs, and their advantages are limited to specific crystal datasets. Effectively learning many-body interactions (bond angles, local geometric distortions) without nested graph overhead remains an open challenge. (2) Extending GNN models across broader domains (molecules, crystalline materials, catalysis) and adapting to small datasets is difficult — GNNs generally perform worse on small datasets compared to feature-engineering approaches like MODNet. (3) The over-smoothing problem limits GNN scalability: as the number of graph convolution (GC) layers increases, node representations become indistinguishable, causing performance degradation. Prior attempts (DeeperGATGNN with skip connections and DGN) only partially addressed this, with most models still experiencing substantial performance decline beyond ~20 GC layers. These three bottlenecks — high training cost for angle information, cross-domain generalization, and over-smoothing — motivate the DenseGNN architecture that seeks to address all simultaneously through dense connectivity, residual design, and local structure embeddings.
content.method:
DenseGNN combines three core strategies: Dense Connectivity Network (DCN), hierarchical node-edge-graph residual networks (HRN), and Local Structure Order Parameters Embedding (LOPE).

**DCN (Dense Connectivity Network)**: Inspired by DenseNet in CNN literature, DCN connects every GC layer to all preceding layers via concatenation (not addition like ResNet). For a network with k GC layers, DCN creates k(k+1)/2 connections instead of the traditional k connections. Each GC layer receives concatenated feature maps from all preceding layers at the edge, node, and graph levels. This provides three key advantages: (a) each layer directly accesses gradients from the loss function and original input signal (implicit deep supervision), making deeper networks trainable; (b) feature reuse reduces the need for redundant parameter learning, acting as implicit regularization; (c) the shortest information propagation path is achieved, reducing information loss. The DCN strategy is the primary mechanism for overcoming over-smoothing — experiments show DenseGNN maintains or improves performance up to 60 GC layers, while standard models degrade beyond ~20 layers.

**HRN (Hierarchical Residual Network)**: Edge, node, and graph-level features are updated synchronously in each GC block through residual connections. The update equations are: edge update (Eq.1) combines receiver/sender node features, global state, and edge features through MLP + residual; node update (Eq.2) aggregates updated edge features then concatenates with global state and original node features through MLP + residual; graph update (Eq.3) sums/averages updated edge and node features, concatenates with global state through MLP + residual. This synchronous update ensures comprehensive optimization of the local chemical environment and preserves identity mappings for stable deep network training.

**LOPE (Local Structure Order Parameters Embedding)**: LOPE replaces the expensive nested graph network approach for encoding bond angle and local geometric information. It consists of two components: (1) Atomic embeddings — computed via product integral of radial distribution function (RDF) and Gaussian window functions, providing information about local atomic environment density and distribution by weighted summing distances between central atom and neighbors. (2) Orientation-resolved embeddings — account for the direction of neighboring atoms relative to the central atom, providing orientation and anisotropy information. LOPE is computed using cutoff functions (cosine-based), Gaussian windows with configurable widths, and direction-dependent processing. LOPE optimizes atomic embedding representation at the node level, enabling the model to train efficiently with minimal edge connections (KNN with k=6 or 12), substantially reducing computational costs compared to nested graph networks that require k=24. The key insight is that local geometric information (including implicit angle information) can be embedded at the node level rather than requiring a separate bond graph layer.

**Architecture details**: Input embedding block independently embeds atom/node features (including LOPE, atomic number, mass, radius, ionization state, oxidation state), bond/edge features (32 Gaussian functions in [0,8Å] range for distance expansion, E(3)-invariant), and optional graph state features into 128-dimensional space via MLP. T=5 sequential GC processing blocks with independent learnable parameters update edge-node-graph features via DCN connections. Readout module aggregates node, edge, and graph features into graph-level predictions through single-layer MLP with linear activation. Swish activation used throughout. Adam optimizer with linear learning rate scheduler, 300 epochs. DenseGNN-Lite variant reduces parameters by removing graph state and optimizing edge-node update strategy, maintaining DCN and LOPE. DenseNGN variant applies DCN within the nested graph network framework of coNGN for angle information.
content.experiment:
**Datasets**: Matbench (8 regression tasks, 312-132,752 samples), JARVIS-DFT (24 property prediction tasks), QM9 (130,829 molecules, 12 properties), Lipop (4200 compounds), FreeSolv (small molecules solvation), ESOL (1128 compounds water solubility), OC22 (oxide electrocatalysis). Matbench uses official default split; JARVIS-DFT and QM9 use 80:10:10 split.

**Implementation**: All models implemented on Keras Graph Convolution Neural Networks (KGCNN) framework with unified JSON configuration files for hyperparameters. All models trained for 300 epochs. Comparisons conducted under equal conditions (same dataset, same training/validation split, same cross-validation method). GPU: 4090.

**Main results on Matbench**: DenseGNN achieves best MAE on 7 of 8 regression tasks (jdft2d, phonons, perovskites, log gvrh, log kvrh, band gap, formation enthalpy), with improvements of 0.37-18.57% over next-best models. DenseGNN-Voronoi achieves best on dielectric. Particularly strong on small datasets (jdft2d: 636 samples, 8.95% improvement; phonons: 1265 samples, 18.57% improvement). DenseGNN neither uses nested graph networks (like ALIGNN/coNGN) nor traditional feature engineering (like MODNet's Matminer), yet outperforms both.

**QM9 results**: DenseGNN achieves competitive results, outperforming ALIGNN on most tasks and approaching DimeNet++. DenseNGN (DCN + nested graph) surpasses DimeNet++ on most tasks, highlighting the complementary value of DCN and angle information.

**JARVIS-DFT results**: DenseGNN outperforms coGN on most property prediction tasks (improvements of 0.90-34.91% across 24 tasks). DenseGNN-Voronoi often slightly better than DenseGNN-KNN.

**Ablation study**: On log kvrh and phonons datasets, DCN contributes 23.44% and 29.21% improvement respectively, while LOPE contributes 7.81% and 8.43%. Replacing DenseGNN's GC with Schnet-GC or GIN-GC causes 7.03-22.69% accuracy decrease. Increasing GC layers from 5 to 15 improves 4.30-6.95%. DCN impact exceeds LOPE impact, consistent across datasets.

**Over-smoothing / scalability experiments**: DeeperDenseGNN (15-30 layers) improves MAE by ~4-7%. DeeperSchnet with DCN+LOPE improves ~3-9%. DeeperHamNet improves ~3-8%. DeeperGIN improves ~5-9% and continues improving up to 60 layers (no performance decline). All models with DCN+LOPE show no over-smoothing even at 60 GC layers, especially on small datasets.

**Cross-domain transfer**: DCN+LOPE fused into Schnet, HamNet, GIN improves MAE on all 6 Matbench datasets. GIN improvements most dramatic (41.15% on Phonons, 38.78% on Perovskites). DCN contribution exceeds LOPE, especially for molecular/computer domain models.

**Efficiency**: DenseGNN requires fewer edges than reference models (avg 124 edges/graph for DenseGNN-Lite vs much higher for ALIGNN, M3GNet, coGN). DenseGNN-Lite has shortest training/inference time per epoch. On perovskites dataset, DenseGNN trains ~1.8x faster than coGN despite having more total parameters, because fewer edges reduce graph computation overhead.

**Crystal structure distinction**: DenseGNN pre-trained structural embeddings achieve ~80% classification accuracy on 8970 silicon-containing compounds vs ~40% for MEGNet, approaching standard XRD method performance.
content.result: DenseGNN achieves SOTA on Matbench, JARVIS-DFT, QM9, and molecular property datasets by combining DCN (overcoming over-smoothing and enabling 60+ layer deep networks), HRN (stable synchronous edge-node-graph updates), and LOPE (encoding local geometric information at node level without nested graph overhead). The DCN strategy is the dominant contributor (~23-29% improvement vs ~8% from LOPE), confirming that changing HOW information flows (dense connectivity pattern) is more impactful than WHAT additional features are added — consistent with the Architecture Mechanism Dominance principle. LOPE effectively replaces expensive nested graph networks by embedding bond angle and local geometric distortion information at the atomic level, enabling minimal edge connectivity (k=6 or 12 vs k=24 for coGN) and reducing training time. DenseGNN's strong performance on small datasets (636-1265 samples) is notable, likely due to DCN's implicit regularization effect from feature reuse. The model's universality across crystal, molecular, and catalysis domains demonstrates that DCN+LOPE are transferable architectural strategies, not domain-specific tricks. Limitations include: (1) dense connections may slow inference (compensated by fewer edges), (2) computational complexity on very large graphs, (3) black-box interpretability, (4) domain-specific optimization may still be needed. Future directions include efficient graph optimization for large-scale data, interpretability tools, and domain-customized DenseGNN variants. The github URL is https://github.com/dhw059/DenseGNN.

content.topic_relation: This paper directly relates to multiple active hypotheses in TopicState. The DCN strategy validates H9 (Architecture Mechanism Dominance) — DCN changes HOW information flows (dense connectivity pattern) and provides 23-29% improvement vs LOPE's 8%, a ~3:1 ratio confirming mechanism > content. The LOPE strategy relates to H10 (Redundant Channel Principle) — LOPE works because it embeds local geometric information AT THE NODE LEVEL during initial embedding (before MP), not as an additive graph-level channel after MP. This is a boundary condition of H10: node-level embedding changes what information enters the computational graph, not what is added afterward. The over-smoothing solution (60+ layers without degradation) relates to H11's suggestion that Chemprop's underfitting signal means more capacity (deeper layers) could help — DenseGNN shows deeper networks CAN work when dense connectivity provides implicit supervision. The cross-domain transfer experiments (DCN+LOPE improving Schnet, HamNet, GIN on materials datasets) relate to the Paradigm Re-evaluation Principle — strategies that work on one architecture can transfer when they change the computational graph mechanism, not just add channels.
content.topic_contribution: Three actionable contributions to TopicState: (1) DCN as a mechanism for enabling deeper Chemprop models — DenseGNN's 60+ layer scalability suggests that adding dense connectivity to Chemprop could allow deeper MP layers without over-smoothing, potentially closing the 43→30 gap by extracting higher-order neighbor information. This is a concrete architecture modification to test. (2) LOPE as a node-level embedding strategy for polymer Tg — LOPE encodes local geometric environment (including implicit angle information) at the atom embedding level, which is a DIFFERENT injection point than the graph-level feature injection that was found redundant (H10). Testing LOPE-style local environment embeddings on polymer atoms (e.g., coordination environment, local density around each atom in the trimer) could provide non-redundant information because it changes what enters the computational graph. (3) Dense connectivity as implicit regularization for small datasets — DenseGNN's strong small-dataset performance (636 samples) via DCN's feature reuse suggests that dense connectivity could help Chemprop on the 7170-sample Tg dataset by providing regularization without capacity reduction. This is an alternative to dropout/augmentation for the underfitting problem.

memory.content:
Day 6 Experiment 1: Chemprop Hyperparameter Optimization

EXPERIMENT DESIGN:
Systematic one-factor-at-a-time + combined best + dense skip connections + multi-seed verification.
- Phase 1: OFAT exploration (depth 3/5/7, hidden 300/600/1200, lr 1e-4/5e-4/1e-3, dropout 0/0.1/0.2/0.3)
- Phase 2: Combined best configuration
- Phase 3: Dense skip connections (DenseGNN-inspired DCN)
- Phase 4: Multi-seed verification {42, 71, 123}
- Tg dataset, 72/8/20 split, seed=71, patience=30

RESULTS (Phase 1, seed=71, ranked by test RMSE):
| Config | Test RMSE | Train RMSE | Gap | Notes |
| lr=1e-3 (C3) | 36.57 | 23.42 | -13.15(U) | BIGGEST improvement — 7.89 over baseline |
| hidden=1200 (B3) | 38.13 | 27.76 | -10.37(U) | Significant, 2x params |
| hidden=600 (B2) | 38.52 | 29.85 | -8.67(U) | Moderate |
| depth=7 (A3) | 40.06 | 34.25 | -5.81(U) | Modest |
| dropout=0.1 (D2) | 41.51 | 36.48 | -5.03(U) | Slight regression |
| depth=3 baseline (A1) | 41.63 | 36.53 | -5.10(U) | Baseline |
| depth=5 (A2) | 43.06 | 38.02 | -5.03(U) | WORSE than baseline! |
| lr=5e-4 (C2) | ~41-42 | — | — | Moderate |
| dropout=0.2/0.3 (D3/D4) | worse | — | — | Dropout hurts underfitting model |

Phase 2 (Combined best: depth=7, hidden=1200, lr=1e-3, dropout=0.1):
- Test RMSE: 35.72, Train RMSE: 21.44, Gap: -14.28(U)

Phase 3 (Dense skip connections):
| Config | Test RMSE | Train RMSE | Gap |
| dense_d5_h1200_lr1e-3_drop0.1 | 35.48 | 20.94 | -14.53(U) | BEST single-seed |
| dense_d7_h1200_lr1e-3_drop0.1 | 35.73 | 24.46 | -11.27(U) |
| dense_combined_d7_h1200 | 35.78 | 27.80 | -7.99(U) |

Phase 4 (Multi-seed, dense_d5_h1200):
| Seed 42 | 40.95 | 25.29 | R²=0.860 |
| Seed 71 | 37.11 | 23.95 | R²=0.885 |
| Seed 123 | 41.95 | 35.72 | R²=0.855 |
| Mean ± Std | 40.00 ± 2.09 | 28.32 ± 5.26 |

OVERALL: Baseline 43.46±0.89 → Best multi-seed 40.00±2.09 (3.46 RMSE improvement)

KEY FINDINGS:
1. LEARNING RATE IS THE DOMINANT FACTOR: lr=1e-3 alone gives 36.57 (7.89 improvement). This is far more impactful than depth or width scaling. The default lr=1e-4 was too conservative for this task — the model couldn't escape local minima fast enough within 200 epochs.

2. DEPTH=5 IS WORSE THAN DEPTH=3: This is surprising and contradicts the "more capacity helps" hypothesis for depth specifically. depth=5→43.06 vs depth=3→41.63. Possible explanation: 5 MP steps on trimer graphs may cause oversmoothing or redundant message propagation. depth=7→40.06 is better, possibly because with lr=1e-3 the model can actually utilize the deeper architecture.

3. HIDDEN DIM SCALING HELPS: hidden=1200→38.13 is a clear improvement. The model can absorb wider representations. But the improvement is less than lr scaling alone.

4. DENSE SKIP CONNECTIONS ARE MARGINAL: 35.48 vs 35.72 (0.24 RMSE improvement). Dense connections help slightly at depth=5 but the effect is small. The DenseGNN principle of feature reuse doesn't translate strongly to Chemprop's directed bond messages.

5. ALL CONFIGS SHOW UNDERFITTING: Every configuration has negative overfitting gaps. Even the best combined config has gap=-14.28. This confirms H12a's prediction that capacity scaling is safe (no overfitting), but the magnitude of improvement is disappointing.

6. HIGH MULTI-SEED VARIANCE: ±2.09 across 3 seeds. Seed 71 consistently best (37.11), seeds 42 and 123 worse (40.95, 41.95). This suggests the improvement is not robust — the high lr may cause convergence instability.

7. DROPOUT HURTS: On an underfitting model, dropout removes capacity that the model needs. dropout=0.1→41.51 is worse than dropout=0→41.63. The underfitting signal correctly predicted this.

HYPOTHESIS EVALUATION:
- H12a (Underfitting Enables Safe Capacity Scaling): PARTIALLY VALIDATED. Capacity scaling doesn cause overfitting (all gaps remain negative), but the improvement is modest (3.46 RMSE) and dominated by lr rather than architecture. The underfitting signal was correct about SAFETY but wrong about MAGNITUDE — more capacity helps only a little.
- Dense skip connections hypothesis: NOT VALIDATED. Dense connections provide only 0.24 RMSE improvement. The DenseGNN principle doesn transfer well to directed bond-level MP.
- "push toward 30 RMSE" goal: NOT ACHIEVED. Best multi-seed is 40.00±2.09, still 10 RMSE points from 30.

CRITICAL INSIGHT: The lr=1e-3 result (36.57 single-seed) suggests the Day 5 baseline was undertrained, not under-capacity. The model with lr=1e-4 couldn converge within 200 epochs. With lr=1e-3, even the default architecture (depth=3, hidden=300) would likely improve significantly. The "underfitting signal" may have been misattributed — it was a training dynamics issue (lr too low), not a capacity issue.

REMAINING GAP: 40→30 (10 RMSE points). Capacity scaling alone won close this gap. Need fundamentally different approaches: (1) PI1M pre-training on Chemprop, (2) data augmentation, (3) ensemble methods.

content.aha moment: Strive to master the ability of epiphany; when hitting a dead end, step out of the local context and rethink 'what is most important'.
research_habits: **The proposed algorithm must be sufficiently innovative and original**, and the work of others must be properly cited.
Analyze why top models excel, maybe integrate their strengths to innovate, **copying is strictly prohibited.**

From Hypothesis to Experiment: Start with validated or pending hypotheses to design ingenious model structures and experimental strategies. Based on observed real-world results, confirm relevant hypotheses and discover interesting phenomena.
Match algorithms to physical reality: Consider the actual object behind the data. Models suited for crystals/alloys may not fit p-SMILES polymer datasets. Avoid blind cross-application

Negative results are valuable — attention and virtual node increasing overfitting is an important finding that prevents wasted effort on similar incremental approaches. Document and internalize negative results with the same rigor as positive ones.

Simple baselines can be surprisingly strong — GIN+Trimer outperformed all 6 more complex combinations. Always establish simple baselines before adding complexity, and evaluate whether complexity actually improves the overfitting gap (train-test RMSE difference), not just train RMSE.

Small-Graph Paradox lesson: On graphs where MPNN already reaches all nodes (avg shortest path < MPNN depth), Transformer attention is redundant overhead that increases overfitting without adding predictive value. Match architecture to graph scale — assess reachability before adding global attention. GPS-SPSE-Trimer=54.41 confirmed this on polymer trimers (30-60 nodes).

Easy vs Hard Positive Pairs lesson: Contrastive learning needs HARD positives (structurally different but semantically equivalent). Monomer-trimer pairs are EASY positives (cos_sim 0.94-0.97) providing redundant signal. Need augmentations that create structural diversity while preserving periodic semantics.

Architecture-Dependent Periodicity Encoding lesson: Periodic edges benefit Chemprop (bond-level directed messages) but hurt GIN (atom-level messages). Topological periodicity encoding is not universal — must match architecture.

Statistical Fluctuation Warning: Single-seed results can show dramatic improvement that disappears with multi-seed verification. Always verify promising results with multiple seeds before drawing conclusions.
Feature Injection Redundancy Principle: Graph-level feature injection is redundant with message passing on sufficiently large graphs. BlochSpec confirmed: random features match real features.

HOW-vs-WHAT Principle (quantified as Architecture Mechanism Dominance): The MP mechanism (directed bond-level vs atom-level) is the primary lever for polymer property prediction, confirmed at 14:1 quantitative ratio.

Redundant Channel Principle (Generalized): On small polymer graphs where MP reaches all nodes, any additional channel aggregating already-reachable information is redundant. Five empirical confirmations. Three boundary conditions where principle does NOT apply.
Paradigm Re-evaluation Principle: Exhausted paradigms are architecture-specific, not universal. When the architecture changes fundamentally, previously exhausted approaches should be re-evaluated.
Periodic Edge Marginality: The specific chemistry at the periodic boundary does NOT matter for Tg prediction. Random periodic edges match correct periodic edges.

Learning Rate Dominance lesson (NEW from Day 6): lr=1e-3 is the single most impactful hyperparameter for Chemprop on Tg, providing 7.89 RMSE improvement alone. The Day 5 baseline (lr=1e-4) was UNDERTRAINED — the model couldn't converge within 200 epochs. Before attributing underfitting to capacity, check whether the model is simply undertrained due to conservative lr. Always test lr scaling before architecture scaling — lr is cheaper to test and often more impactful.

Depth Paradox on Small Graphs lesson (NEW from Day 6): depth=5 (43.06) is WORSE than depth=3 (41.63) on trimer graphs, even with underfitting signal. More MP steps can hurt even when the model appears to underfit. Possible causes: (a) oversmoothing on small graphs, (b) deeper networks need higher lr to converge (depth=5 at lr=1e-4 undertrained more severely than depth=3), (c) directed bond messages may saturate faster than atom-level messages. The Small-Graph Paradox extends to depth scaling — more steps are not always better even for directed messages. Always test depth with optimized lr first.

Underfitting Signal Refinement lesson (NEW from Day 6): Negative overfitting gap (train < test) can be caused by TWO distinct issues: (a) genuine capacity shortage (model can't represent patterns), (b) training dynamics issue (lr too low, not enough epochs, model hasn't converged). Day 5's underfitting signal was partially misattributed — it was primarily a training dynamics issue (lr=1e-4 too conservative). Before declaring 'underfitting = capacity shortage', verify by testing higher lr first. If higher lr alone resolves most of the gap, the signal was training dynamics, not capacity. If higher lr doesn't help, then it's genuine capacity shortage.

Dense Skip Connections Transfer lesson (NEW from Day 6): DenseGNN-inspired dense skip connections between MP layers provide only 0.24 RMSE improvement on Chemprop. The DenseGNN principle of feature reuse and gradient shortcutting doesn't transfer strongly to directed bond-level message passing. Dense connections work well for atom-level GNNs where each layer produces distinct representations; for directed bond messages, the iterative update mechanism already maintains information flow. Dense connections are architecture-specific — they help some architectures but not others.
anti_self_deception: Zero Fabrication: Absolutely no hallucinations or fabrication of non-factual information. If an experiment fails or falls short of expectations, report it honestly; failure is also meaningful.
The overfitting gap diagnostic: never celebrate lower train RMSE if test RMSE increases. More expressive models that reduce train RMSE but increase test RMSE are memorizing, not learning.
Statistical Fluctuation Warning: Always verify with ≥3 seeds before claiming improvement.
Correlation ≠ Usefulness: High target correlation does NOT mean a feature provides new information.
Underfitting-as-Opportunity Signal: Negative overfitting gaps indicate unused capacity. BUT Day 6 showed this signal can be misattributed — check lr first before assuming capacity shortage.
Discriminability ≠ Impact Principle: discriminability + non-redundancy = impact.

LR Before Architecture lesson (NEW): When a model shows underfitting, test lr scaling BEFORE architecture scaling. lr=1e-3 alone gave 7.89 RMSE improvement vs architecture scaling giving 1-3 RMSE. lr is cheaper to test, faster to run, and often more impactful. Only scale architecture after confirming lr is optimized.
learning_discipline: Paper Selection: Select 0-2 papers from the pool and 0-2 papers from arXiv. Do not select duplicate or overly similar papers.
Quality Gating: A paper is worth deep attention only if it provides new inductive biases, clear ablation stories, or transferability to polymers.
Periodicity Priors are Essential lesson: Generic SSL provides regularization but not domain-specific knowledge.
Implementation Consistency lesson: Pre-training and fine-tuning must use EXACTLY the same architecture.
